title: Safe practical work: choosing equipment, naming risks, judging predictions

summary.text: You want to know how long a spoon of sugar takes to vanish in warm water. Which spoon, which cup and which clock will you use, and what could go wrong before you even begin? In this lesson you choose your own equipment and learn to use it the right way. You name the risks of a test and plan how to make each one smaller. Then you write a prediction, which is a guess with a reason, and use your results to say how close it was.
summary.art: A child at a table with a steel tumbler on a tray, a teaspoon, a phone stopwatch and a notebook that says 'I predict 40 seconds'.

intro.hook: Put a ruler, a teaspoon, a big steel pot and a phone on the table. Your job is to find out how much water a small bottle cap holds. Which of these would you pick up, and which would you leave?
intro.text: A test done with your hands is called practical work. Before any practical work, a scientist makes three choices. She chooses the tools that fit the job. She thinks about what could hurt someone, and how to stop that. And she says what she expects to happen, so that the result can surprise her. Today you make all three choices yourself, and then you check how good your expectation was.
intro.art: A table with a ruler, a teaspoon, a big steel pot, a phone and one small bottle cap in the middle, with a child's hand hovering over them.

outcomes: I can pick the right equipment for a job from a set, and say why it fits.
I can use a ruler, a measuring cup, a thermometer and a stopwatch the right way.
I can tell a hazard from a risk, and name the risks in a test before I start.
I can plan how to make each risk smaller, and carry out the test safely.
I can make a prediction with a reason, for something I know and for something new to me.
I can use my results to say how close my prediction was.
I can say what a missed prediction might be telling me.

explanations.concept: Practical work is finding out with your hands, and equipment is whatever helps you do it
explanations.definition: Practical work is a test or an observation that you carry out yourself. Equipment is the set of things you use to carry it out.
explanations.description: You can find some things out by thinking, and some by asking. Other things you can only find out by doing. Will a wet towel dry faster hung up or folded? You have to try it. That trying is practical work. The things you use are your equipment: a towel, a clothes line, a clock, a notebook. Equipment does not have to come from a laboratory. A steel tumbler is equipment when you measure with it. A window sill is equipment when you grow a seed there. What makes something equipment is the job you give it.
examples: A kitchen weighing scale becomes science equipment when you weigh a sponge dry and then wet.
A phone becomes equipment three times over: a stopwatch, a torch and a camera.
A cook testing if the dosa pan is hot enough by sprinkling water is doing practical work.
explanations.one_view: This card only says what the two words mean in this lesson. The different views about tools and the senses come in later cards.
explanations.art: A kitchen shelf where a tumbler, a spoon, a scale and a clock each wear a small label saying 'equipment'.
explanations.context: This card says what practical work and equipment are, so the rest of the lesson can use both words.

explanations.concept: Each measuring tool answers one kind of question
explanations.definition: A measuring tool is built to measure one quantity. Choosing equipment starts with asking which quantity you need.
explanations.description: A quantity is something you can measure and give a number to. Length is a quantity, and a ruler or a tape measures it. Volume is how much space a liquid takes up, and a measuring cup measures it. Mass is how much stuff is in a thing, and a weighing scale measures it. Temperature is how hot or cold something is, and a thermometer measures it. Time is measured with a clock or a stopwatch. So the first question when you choose equipment is 'What do I need to know?' Suppose you need to know how hot the water is. A ruler cannot help, however good the ruler is.
examples: How tall is the bean plant today? Length, so a ruler, in centimetres.
How much water did the sponge soak up? Volume, so a measuring cup, in millilitres.
How heavy is one idli before and after steaming? Mass, so a kitchen scale, in grams.
How long does the ice take to melt? Time, so a clock, in minutes.
explanations.one_view: Which tool measures which quantity is agreed everywhere, so there is only one honest view here.
explanations.art: Five tools in a row, a ruler, a measuring cup, a kitchen scale, a thermometer and a stopwatch, each joined by a line to the question it answers.
explanations.context: This card matches each common tool to the one question it can answer.

explanations.concept: The tool must fit the size of the thing: look at the smallest mark
explanations.definition: The smallest mark on a tool is the smallest amount it can measure. Choose a tool whose smallest mark is much smaller than the amount you are measuring.
explanations.description: Two tools can measure the same quantity and still not be equally good for your job. A one-litre kitchen jug often has a mark only every 100 millilitres. A medicine cup has a mark every 5 millilitres or less. If you need 10 millilitres of water, the jug cannot show it, and the medicine cup can. The same goes for time. A wall clock with no seconds hand cannot time a toy car that rolls for 3 seconds. A tool that is too fine is also a poor fit. Nobody measures a room 6 metres long with a 15 centimetre ruler, because laying it down 40 times adds 40 small mistakes.
examples: A school ruler has a mark every 1 millimetre. A tailor's tape has the same marks but bends round a tree trunk, so the tape fits that job.
A kitchen scale that shows whole grams cannot weigh one grain of rice. Weigh a hundred grains together, then divide the total by a hundred.
A phone stopwatch shows hundredths of a second, but your thumb takes about two tenths of a second to press. So the last digit means little when a person does the pressing.
explanations.one_view: This is a rule of measuring that every instrument maker and scientist uses, so there is only one honest view.
explanations.art: A big jug and a small medicine cup side by side, each holding 10 millilitres of water, with the jug's water far below its first mark.
explanations.context: This card shows how to choose between two tools that measure the same thing.

explanations.concept: Using a tool the right way: start at zero, read at eye level, keep it steady
explanations.definition: A tool gives a true reading only when it is used the way it was made to be used.
explanations.description: The right tool, used the wrong way, gives a wrong number. Three habits fix most mistakes. First, start at zero. On many rulers the zero mark is a little way in from the end, so line up the mark and not the edge. Press the zero button on a kitchen scale after you put the empty bowl on. Second, read at eye level. Put a measuring cup on a flat table and bring your eye down to the water line. Looked at from above, the water seems to stand at a different mark. Third, keep the tool steady and wait. A thermometer needs about a minute in the water before its number stops changing.
examples: In a narrow clear tube, the surface of water curves up at the sides. Read the bottom of the curve.
Hold a thermometer by its top end. If you hold the tip, the thermometer measures your fingers.
Say 'three, two, one, go' so the hand that drops and the thumb that times start together.

perspectives.who: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana, chapter 9, an Indian book of surgery whose oldest parts are more than 2,000 years old
perspectives.explanation: A student must practise each tool before using it on a person. The book tells the student to practise cuts on gourds, watermelons and cucumbers, and stitching on cloth and soft leather. It says that even a well-read student is unfit for the work without this practice.

perspectives.who: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana, chapter 7
perspectives.explanation: The same book lists 101 blunt instruments. It then says that the hand is the most important instrument of all, because no other instrument can work without it.

explanations.art: A child crouching so that her eye is level with the water line in a measuring cup on a table, with a dotted line from eye to mark.
explanations.context: This card gives the three habits that make a tool tell the truth: zero, eye level and steadiness.

explanations.concept: Your senses are equipment too, and they compare more than they measure
explanations.definition: Skin, eyes, ears, nose and tongue report how a thing differs from what they met just before. A measuring tool reports against a fixed scale.
explanations.description: Try this with three bowls of water: one cold, one warm from the tap and one in between. Keep one hand in the cold bowl and the other in the warm bowl for one minute. Then put both hands into the middle bowl. The same water feels warm to one hand and cool to the other. Your skin was not wrong. Skin reports change, and each hand came from a different starting point. A thermometer put in the middle bowl gives one number, whichever bowl it came from. That is why scientists use tools for numbers. It is also why they still use their senses to notice that something is worth measuring.
examples: A room feels dark when you walk in from the sun and bright when you wake at night, though the lamp is the same.
After a sweet laddu, a sweet orange tastes sour.

perspectives.who: John Locke, an English philosopher, in 'An Essay Concerning Human Understanding', book 2, chapter 8, in 1690
perspectives.explanation: He described this same test with two hands and one bowl. He concluded that warm and cold, as we feel them, are not in the water in the way that its amount is. They arise where the water meets the hand.

perspectives.who: Skilled craftspeople, such as tea tasters in Assam and the Nilgiris, and potters who judge a kiln by the colour of its flame
perspectives.explanation: With years of practice, senses become fine instruments. A trained taster can tell teas apart that no simple machine can. Their view is that a sense is a tool that must be trained and checked, like any other.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study other animals' senses
perspectives.explanation: Every being has their own equipment. A pit viper senses the warmth of a mouse from a distance. A bee sees ultraviolet marks on a flower, a kind of light that human eyes cannot see. No being's senses report the whole world.

explanations.art: Three bowls in a row with a child's two hands going from the outer bowls into the middle one, and a thermometer in the middle bowl showing one number.
explanations.context: This card shows why a number needs a tool, by letting two hands disagree about the same water.

explanations.concept: A hazard is a thing that could hurt, and a risk is the chance that it will
explanations.definition: A hazard is anything that could cause harm. A risk is how likely the harm is, together with how bad it would be.
explanations.description: A kitchen knife is a hazard, because it is sharp. That is true when it lies in a closed drawer and when a running child carries it. But the risk is very different in the two cases. In the drawer the chance of a cut is tiny. In the running child's hand the chance is high, and the cut could be deep. So a hazard is about the thing. A risk is about the thing, the person, the place and what is being done. This is good news, because you often cannot change the hazard. Water for tea must be hot. You can nearly always change the risk.
examples: Hazard: hot water. Low risk: half a tumbler of warm tap water on a tray. High risk: a full pot of boiling water at the table's edge.
Hazard: a glass jar can break. The risk rises on a tiled floor and falls on a mat.
Hazard: the Sun can harm eyes. The risk is high if you look at the Sun, and low if you watch its shadow.
explanations.one_view: These are working definitions that safety workers around the world share, so there is only one honest view of the two words.
explanations.art: The same knife drawn twice: resting in a closed drawer with a small 'low risk' tag, and in the hand of a running child with a large 'high risk' tag.
explanations.context: This card separates two words that people mix up, hazard and risk, because the rest of the lesson needs both.

explanations.concept: Naming the risks before you start: what could hurt, whom, and how badly
explanations.definition: A risk assessment is a short list you make before a test. It says what could cause harm, who could be harmed, and how likely and how bad the harm would be.
explanations.description: Before a test, walk through it in your head from the first step to the cleaning up. At each step ask three questions. What here could hurt someone? Who could be hurt: me, a helper, a baby who crawls in, a pet, the plant? How likely is it, and how bad would it be? Write each answer in a line. Scientists call this list a risk assessment. Most home tests have the same few hazards. They are heat, sharp edges, glass, small things that could be swallowed, wall sockets, water on the floor, and the Sun in the eyes. Naming them takes two minutes. A risk that has a name is much easier to plan for.
examples: Test: dissolving sugar in warm water. Risks named: a scald from water that is too hot, a slip on spilled water, a broken glass.
Test: growing moong seeds. Risks named: a toddler swallowing seeds, mouldy seeds touched and then fingers in the mouth.
Test: making shadows. Risk named: looking straight at the Sun.
explanations.one_view: Listing risks before work is standard practice in schools, laboratories and workshops. People differ on how much risk to accept, and that debate is in a later card.
explanations.art: A notebook page with three columns headed 'What could hurt?', 'Who?' and 'How likely, how bad?', filled in by a child for a warm-water test.
explanations.context: This card gives the three questions that turn a vague worry into a list of named risks.

explanations.concept: Making a risk smaller: remove, swap, separate, protect
explanations.definition: There are four ways to make a risk smaller. You can remove the hazard, swap it for a safer one, put a barrier or distance between it and people, or wear protection. The first ways work better than the last.
explanations.description: Once a risk has a name, there are four kinds of plan, and they are not equally strong. The strongest is to remove the hazard. If the test works with cold water, use cold water. The next is to swap. Use a plastic or steel tumbler in place of glass, and warm tap water in place of boiling water. The third is to separate people from the hazard. Work on a tray in the middle of the table, and keep a baby in another room. The weakest is protection that you wear, such as an apron or glasses, because the hazard is still there and the protection can slip. Safety engineers call this order the hierarchy of controls.
examples: A torch in place of a candle removes the flame from a shadow test.
A tray under the cups means a spill stays on the tray and not on the floor.
Tied-back hair and rolled-up sleeves keep loose things away from the work.
A grown-up pouring the warm water is separation too: the child is kept apart from the pouring.
explanations.one_view: The order from removing down to wearing protection is used by safety bodies in most countries. The open question is how far to go, which the card on zero risk takes up.
explanations.art: Four steps going down like a staircase, labelled remove, swap, separate and protect, each with a small picture: no flame, a steel tumbler, a tray, an apron.
explanations.context: This card gives four ways to shrink a named risk, in order from strongest to weakest.

explanations.concept: Carrying out the work safely: the habits that matter while your hands are busy
explanations.definition: Working safely means keeping to the plan while you work, and stopping when something happens that the plan did not cover.
explanations.description: A plan on paper protects nobody unless the hands follow it. A few habits do most of the work. Clear the table of everything the test does not need. Put each thing back in its own place after you use it. Never taste anything in a test unless the test is about taste and a grown-up has said the food is safe. To smell something, hold it away and wave a little air towards your nose. Wipe a spill at once. Wash your hands at the end. And the most important habit is this: if something happens that you did not expect, stop. Step back, tell someone, and think again before you carry on.
examples: The water from the tap comes out hotter than you planned. Stop, add cold water, and test the warmth with a thermometer or with a grown-up's hand before going on.
A cup cracks. Stop, leave the pieces, and fetch a grown-up with a broom.
At the end, pour sugar water down the sink and not into a bottle someone may drink from.
explanations.one_view: These habits are common to school and research laboratories. They are practice, not theory, so there is only one honest view.
explanations.art: A tidy table with only a tray, two cups, a spoon and a notebook on it, and a child wiping up a small spill with a cloth.
explanations.context: This card lists the habits that keep a safe plan safe while the test is going on.

explanations.concept: A checklist catches the slips that skill does not
explanations.definition: A checklist is a short written list of steps that must not be missed, read out and ticked at the moment of doing.
explanations.description: Experts forget simple steps, most of all when the work is familiar. In October 1935 a new and very large aeroplane, the Boeing Model 299, crashed on a test flight in Ohio in the United States. The pilots were among the best in the country. They had forgotten to release a lock on the controls. Pilots then wrote the steps down on a card and read them before every flight. Aeroplanes have used checklists ever since. In 2008 the World Health Organization made a 19-step checklist for operations. It was tried in eight hospitals in eight cities, one of them New Delhi. Deaths after operations fell from 15 in every 1,000 to 8 in every 1,000.
examples: A test checklist for home: table clear, tray down, hair tied, grown-up near for the warm water, cloth ready, prediction written.
A cook's habit of checking the gas knob before leaving the kitchen is a one-line checklist.

perspectives.who: Atul Gawande, a surgeon, and the World Health Organization team, in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2009
perspectives.explanation: Work today has too many steps for memory alone. A short list read aloud catches the missed step, and it also makes the team speak to each other before they start.

perspectives.who: David Urbach and colleagues, who studied 101 hospitals in Ontario, Canada, in 2014
perspectives.explanation: When hospitals across Ontario were required to use the checklist, deaths after operations hardly changed. Their view is that a list by itself does little. It works only when the people using it believe in it and really stop to read it.

perspectives.who: Some experienced surgeons and pilots, when checklists were first brought in
perspectives.explanation: A list treats a skilled person like a beginner, and ticking boxes can take the place of thinking. Attention, they said, is the real safety.

explanations.art: A pilot's hand holding a small card of ticked steps in a cockpit, beside a child's hand holding a similar card over a kitchen table.
explanations.context: This card tells where checklists came from, what they achieved, and why people still argue about them.

explanations.concept: A hazard that nobody knows about cannot be put on the list
explanations.definition: A risk assessment can cover only the hazards that are known at the time. New materials and new methods can carry hazards that are discovered later.
explanations.description: Listing risks has a limit. You can name only what somebody already knows. Carl Wilhelm Scheele, a Swedish chemist, discovered several new substances in the 1770s. He smelled and tasted them, as chemists then did. He died in 1786 at the age of 43, and some historians think his chemicals shortened his life. Marie Curie carried tubes of glowing radium in her pocket. Her notebooks are still radioactive, and the national library of France keeps them in lead-lined boxes. In the 1920s, young women in American factories painted watch dials with radium paint. They were told to point their brushes with their lips. Many fell terribly ill. Five of them, led by Grace Fryer, took the company to court in 1927.
examples: The rule 'never taste anything in a test' exists because of people like Scheele.
When scientists work with something new, they treat it as hazardous until tests show otherwise.

perspectives.who: The dial painters, later called the Radium Girls, and the doctors who stood by them, such as Harrison Martland in 1925
perspectives.explanation: The company's scientists protected themselves with screens and tongs, while telling the painters that the paint was harmless. Their view is that risk is not only about knowledge. It is also about who is told, and who is listened to.

perspectives.who: Historians of science
perspectives.explanation: Curie and Scheele were not careless by the standards of their day. Nobody could have listed a hazard that had not been discovered. The lesson they draw is to stay watchful when a thing is new.

explanations.art: An old notebook resting in a grey lead-lined box with a small radiation sign, and beside it a watch dial with glowing numbers.
explanations.context: This card shows the limit of naming risks: some hazards are not yet known, and some are known but not shared.

explanations.concept: No test has zero risk, so people must decide how much is acceptable
explanations.definition: Risk can be made small but never zero. How small is small enough is a choice people make, and they do not all choose alike.
explanations.description: Even a test with a bowl of cold water has some risk, because someone can slip. Crossing the road to buy the sugar has more. So 'Is it safe?' is never a yes-or-no question. The real questions are how big the risk is, what we gain by doing the test, and who carries the risk. A test that teaches a lot may be worth a small risk. A test that teaches little is not worth a large one. People answer these questions differently, and that is a real disagreement, not a mistake by one side.
examples: Cutting an apple to watch it brown needs a knife. Most families accept that risk with a grown-up cutting.
Boiling water for a test that works just as well with warm tap water is a risk with nothing gained.

perspectives.who: The Rio Declaration of the United Nations, Principle 15, in 1992
perspectives.explanation: Where serious harm to the environment is possible, do not wait for full proof before you act to prevent it. This idea is known as the precautionary principle. Suppose fish start dying in a river below a new factory. Waiting years for proof means years of harm, so the factory is asked to cut its waste now, while scientists study the river.

perspectives.who: Chauncey Starr, an American engineer, in the journal Science in 1969
perspectives.explanation: Every benefit carries some risk, so compare the two with numbers. He found that people accept much larger risks when they choose them freely, such as skiing, than when others impose them.

perspectives.who: People who carry the risk without getting the gain
perspectives.explanation: A sum of risk against benefit can look fine overall while one group gets the benefit and another gets the harm. They ask that the sum always says who is who.

explanations.art: A balance scale with 'what we learn' in one pan and 'what could go wrong' in the other, and three different people each pointing to a different tilt.
explanations.context: This card says why no test is perfectly safe, and lays out three ways people decide how much risk to take.

explanations.concept: The other beings in your test are at risk too
explanations.definition: A risk assessment counts every living being the test touches, not only people.
explanations.description: Many tests at home use living beings. There may be a potted plant, sprouting seeds, ants on a wall, a snail from the balcony or the curd bacteria in a bowl. Each of them can be harmed by the test, so they go on the list. Ask what the test will do to them, and how to do less. Watch ants where they already walk, and do not shut them in a jar. If a test keeps a plant in the dark, keep the plant there for a few days at most. Then bring the plant back to the light. Put a snail back where you found them within the hour. Plants and animals feel, remember and decide. Some scientists call these automatic responses.
examples: To learn what ants like to eat, place a grain of sugar and a grain of salt near their path and watch. No ant needs to be caught.
To test whether seeds need light to sprout, put ten seeds on a damp cloth. Keep some in light and some in a dark cupboard, and plant them all afterwards.

perspectives.who: William Russell and Rex Burch, British scientists, in 'The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique' in 1959
perspectives.explanation: They gave three rules for any test on animals. Replace the animal with something else where you can. Reduce the number of animals. Refine the method so that the animals suffer less. Laboratories across the world now follow these three rules.

perspectives.who: The Acharanga Sutra, book 1, lecture 4, lesson 1, one of the oldest Jain texts
perspectives.explanation: All breathing, existing, living beings should not be killed, treated with violence or tormented. Jain teaching counts plants, and the tiny beings in water and soil, among the living.

perspectives.who: Scientists who use animals in medical research
perspectives.explanation: Some knowledge that saves many lives, human and animal, cannot yet be gained without tests on animals. They accept the three rules and hold that stopping all such tests would cause more suffering than it prevents.

explanations.art: A child lying on the floor watching a line of ants walk past a grain of sugar and a grain of salt, with a notebook and no jar in sight.
explanations.context: This card adds plants, ants and other living beings to the list of those a test could harm.

explanations.concept: A prediction is what you expect to happen, with a reason taken from what you already know
explanations.definition: A prediction is a statement, made before a test, of what the result will be. A scientific prediction comes with a reason.
explanations.description: A guess says what will happen. A prediction also says why you think so. 'The sugar will dissolve faster in warm water' is a guess. Here is a prediction. 'Sugar will dissolve faster in warm water, because I have seen it vanish fast in hot tea and slowly in cold lemon juice'. The reason matters for two things. It lets other people check your thinking. And when the result comes in, it tells you what to learn. If the result matches, the reason has passed one test. If the result does not match, something in the reason needs another look. Write the prediction down before the test, with a number if you can.
examples: I predict the wet towel will dry in about 2 hours on the line, because yesterday a wet shirt took about that long.
I predict the bigger ice cube will take longer to melt, because there is more ice to warm up.

perspectives.who: The Nyaya Sutra of Gautama, book 1, chapter 1, sutra 5, with Vatsyayana's commentary of about the 5th century CE
perspectives.explanation: This Indian text on reasoning names three kinds of inference. The first goes from a cause to what will follow. The commentary's example is seeing dark clouds gather and inferring that rain will come. That is a prediction with a reason.

perspectives.who: The Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana, chapter 11, an Indian book of medicine whose oldest parts are about 2,000 years old
perspectives.explanation: It lists four ways of knowing: trusted teaching, direct seeing, inference, and yukti. Yukti is reasoning that puts many causes together to say what will result. Its example is a crop, which comes from water, ploughing, seed and season together.

explanations.art: A notebook line that reads 'I predict ... because ...' with the word 'because' circled, beside a tumbler of water and a spoon of sugar.
explanations.context: This card says what turns a guess into a scientific prediction: the reason.

explanations.concept: Predicting something new: reason from the nearest thing you know
explanations.definition: To predict something unfamiliar, find a familiar case that is like it. Then ask what should stay the same and what should change.
explanations.description: It is easy to predict what you have seen many times. The real power of science is predicting what nobody has seen. You do it by stepping from the known to the new. You know that sugar dissolves faster in warm water. Now someone hands you rock salt, which you have never tested. Rock salt is like sugar in one way: both dissolve in water. So you predict that warm water will speed rock salt up too. In 1871 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev did this with a metal nobody had found. He reasoned from the metals around its empty place in his table. He predicted that each cubic centimetre of it would weigh about 5.9 grams.
examples: In 1875 the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found the metal, now called gallium. He first measured 4.7 grams. Mendeleev wrote to him that the figure was too low, and that the sample must be impure. Measured again on a purer piece, it came to about 5.9.
You know a metal spoon in hot tea gets hot. Predict what a wooden spoon will do, and say what is the same and what is different.
You know a ball rolls farther on tile than on a mat. Predict what a ball will do on sand.
explanations.one_view: Reasoning from a known case to a new one is how predictions are made in every science. Whether such reasoning can ever be certain is a real debate, taken up in the roots.
explanations.art: A stepping-stone path from a stone marked 'sugar in warm water, tested' to a stone marked 'rock salt in warm water, not yet tested', with a child mid-step.
explanations.context: This card shows how to predict in a situation you have never met, by stepping from a case you know.

explanations.concept: Judging a prediction: write it first, then find the difference from the result
explanations.definition: The accuracy of a prediction is how close it came to the measured result. It is found by taking the difference between the two.
explanations.description: After the test, put the prediction and the result side by side. Suppose you predicted 40 seconds and the sugar took 52. The difference is 12 seconds. Then compare the difference with the size of the result. Being 12 seconds off in 52 is a miss of nearly a quarter. Being 12 seconds off in 10 minutes would be a tiny miss. Say which way you missed as well: 'I predicted too short a time.' All of this works only if the prediction was written before the test. After people see a result, they honestly remember having expected it. Psychologists call this hindsight. A number written in ink does not change.
examples: Predicted: the towel dries in 2 hours. Result: 3 hours. Difference: 1 hour too short, which is one third of the result.
Predicted: the big cube lasts longer. Result: the big cube did last longer. The direction was right, though no number was predicted.
explanations.one_view: Subtracting the prediction from the result is plain arithmetic. What counts as close enough is a separate question, in the next card.
explanations.art: A notebook with two boxed numbers, 'Predicted 40 s' and 'Result 52 s', joined by a bracket labelled 'difference 12 s, too short'.
explanations.context: This card shows how to turn 'was I right?' into a number: the difference between prediction and result.

explanations.concept: How close is close enough depends on the spread of your results and on what the answer is for
explanations.definition: A prediction counts as accurate when its miss is no bigger than the natural spread of repeated results, or small enough for the purpose it serves.
explanations.description: No test gives the same number twice. Do the sugar test three times and you may get 48, 52 and 56 seconds. The results spread over 8 seconds without anything being wrong. So a prediction of 50 seconds is as close as this test can judge. A prediction of 40 is outside the spread, and is a real miss. The purpose matters too. The India Meteorological Department predicts each year's monsoon rain as a percentage of the long-term average. It says that the forecast may be off by about 5 per cent either way. If it forecasts 60 centimetres of rain, the true rain may be anywhere from 57 to 63. A farmer can plan around that. An engineer cutting a part for a rocket engine cannot accept a miss of 5 per cent.
examples: Three results: 48, 52, 56 seconds. Prediction 50: inside the spread, so accurate. Prediction 40: outside, so a miss.
A recipe that says 'about a cup' accepts a large miss. A medicine dose does not.
A forecast of 'rain tomorrow afternoon' is close enough for carrying an umbrella, and not close enough for timing a kite festival to the minute.
explanations.one_view: Comparing a miss with the spread of repeats is the standard method. Each field then sets how small a miss it needs.
explanations.art: A number line from 40 to 60 seconds with three dots at 48, 52 and 56, a shaded band between them, one arrow at 50 inside the band and one at 40 outside.
explanations.context: This card gives a fair way to decide if a prediction was close: compare the miss with how much the results spread anyway.

explanations.concept: A missed prediction asks three questions: was the reason wrong, the tool wrong, or the doing wrong?
explanations.definition: When a result misses a prediction, look in three places, in this order: how the test was done, the equipment, and the idea behind the prediction.
explanations.description: Say you predicted 45 seconds, and the sugar took 90. A miss is information. But what does it tell you? There are three places to look. The doing: did you stir one cup and not the other? The tool: was the spoon heaped one time and level the next? The reason: is your idea about warm water wrong, or missing something? Check them in that order, because the first two are easier to fix.
examples: Your sugar took twice as long as predicted. You then notice that this spoonful had large crystals. The reason was missing something: crystal size matters too.
A plant you predicted would bend to the window grows straight. You check and find the curtain was closed all week. The doing was at fault.

perspectives.who: Pierre Duhem, a French physicist, in 1906
perspectives.explanation: No prediction tests one idea alone. It tests the idea together with the tools, the set-up and many smaller assumptions. A miss says that something in the whole bundle is wrong, and it cannot say which part.

explanations.art: A notebook page with a big question mark and three arrows from it, labelled 'my reason?', 'my tool?' and 'my doing?', each with a small picture.
explanations.context: This card says what to do with a prediction that missed.
explanations.one_view: Checking the doing and the tool before the idea is ordinary practice, and no school of science argues against it. The real argument is about when to give up the idea itself, and that has its own card.

explanations.concept: A miss alone cannot say whether a hidden cause or a wrong rule is to blame: Neptune and Vulcan
explanations.definition: When a prediction misses in a careful test, scientists may look for a hidden cause outside the idea, or change the idea itself. A miss alone does not say which.
explanations.description: Scientists meet the same puzzle as your sugar test, and they do not always agree. By the 1840s the planet Uranus was not where the sums predicted. Astronomers kept Newton's law and blamed an unseen planet. Neptune was found in 1846, close to where they said. Later, Mercury also strayed from the sums, by about one hundredth of a degree each century. Astronomers again predicted an unseen planet, and named it Vulcan. Nobody ever found it. This time the law itself needed changing, and Albert Einstein changed it in 1915.
examples: Your cloth dried much slower than predicted. A hidden cause may be at work, such as a very humid day. Or your rule 'sun means quick' may be too simple, because shade and wind matter too.
A friend's sugar takes twice as long as yours. A hidden cause could be bigger crystals. Or you could ask whether warm water speeds up every kind of sugar equally.

perspectives.who: Karl Popper, a philosopher born in Vienna, in 1934
perspectives.explanation: A scientific idea must risk being wrong. When its prediction fails in a careful test, the honest thing is to give the idea up, and not to keep rescuing it with excuses.

perspectives.who: Imre Lakatos, a Hungarian philosopher, in 1970
perspectives.explanation: Scientists are right to protect a good idea for a while, as they did with Neptune. The test is what the protecting leads to. If it leads to new finds, carry on. If it leads only to more excuses, let go.

explanations.art: A sky chart with two small planets drawn in: Neptune with a tick beside it and Vulcan with a question mark.
explanations.context: This card shows that scientists themselves argue about what a miss means.

explanations.concept: Can everything be predicted? Some things, only a short way ahead
explanations.definition: Some systems, such as the weather, follow fixed laws and still cannot be predicted far ahead, because tiny differences at the start grow into large ones.
explanations.description: If you knew enough, could you predict anything? In 1961 the American weather scientist Edward Lorenz ran a weather sum on his computer twice. The second time he typed one starting number as 0.506 in place of 0.506127. That is a difference of about one part in 4,000. After a short while the two forecasts had nothing in common. He had found that in weather, small differences do not stay small. We can never measure today's air perfectly, so a forecast gets worse with each day ahead. Today's forecasts are useful for about a week, and most weather scientists think two weeks is near the limit. An eclipse, though, can be predicted centuries ahead to the minute. So the reach of prediction depends on the thing being predicted.
examples: A dropped steel spoon: easy to predict where it lands. A dropped sheet of paper: nearly impossible.
Tomorrow's high tide at Chennai can be found in a table printed a year ago. Tomorrow's exact cloud shapes cannot.

perspectives.who: Pierre-Simon Laplace, a French mathematician, in 'A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities' in 1814
perspectives.explanation: Imagine a mind that knew the place and motion of every particle at one moment. For that mind nothing would be uncertain, and the future would be as plain as the past. On this view, what we cannot predict is only what we do not know well enough.

perspectives.who: Edward Lorenz, in 1963, and the scientists of chaos who followed
perspectives.explanation: The laws may be fixed, but perfect knowledge of the start is impossible. So for weather and many other things, long-range prediction is out of reach in practice, however good the computer.

perspectives.who: Most physicists, since the 1920s
perspectives.explanation: Some events seem to have no cause that fixes their moment. In a lump of radioactive material, physics can predict that half the atoms will break up in a certain time. No one can predict which atom will go next. A smaller group of physicists thinks hidden causes exist that we have not found.

explanations.art: Two wavy forecast lines starting from almost the same dot, running together for a short way and then swinging far apart.
explanations.context: This card asks how far ahead prediction can reach, and gives three answers scientists have defended.

explanations.concept: Careful practical work is very old, and India's texts wrote down its rules
explanations.definition: Rules for testing things carefully, choosing instruments and learning from results were written in several ancient cultures, long before modern laboratories.
explanations.description: It is easy to think that careful testing began in Europe a few hundred years ago. The written record says otherwise. The Charaka Samhita, in its Vimanasthana section, chapter 8, tells a physician to examine in an ordered way before acting. It says to judge a claim by reasoning and by what is seen. In Cairo, about 1021 CE, Ibn al-Haytham wrote in his Book of Optics that anyone who studies nature must test what earlier writers say. He added that you must suspect even your own judgement. In China, the Mozi, a book from about the 4th century BCE, gives three tests for any statement. One of them is to check it against what ordinary people's eyes and ears report. The tools have changed. The habits are the same ones this lesson teaches.
examples: The Sushruta Samhita asks that a sharp instrument be so well made and sharpened that it can split a hair.
A potter in Manamadurai, a weaver in Kanchipuram and a cook testing sugar syrup all use rules that were tested many times. These rules passed from hand to hand. Most were never written down.

perspectives.who: Historians who place the start of modern science in Europe in the 1600s
perspectives.explanation: What was new then, they say, was joining tests to mathematics and to instruments, and publishing results so that strangers could repeat them. Earlier work was careful but was not organised in this way.

perspectives.who: Historians such as Joseph Needham, who studied science in China, and Dharampal, who studied science and technology in 18th-century India
perspectives.explanation: Careful, tested knowledge was built in many places by many kinds of people, among them craftspeople, healers and farmers. Much of it was passed on by doing and was never credited, because it was not written in books.

explanations.art: Three open books side by side, one in Sanskrit, one in Arabic and one in Chinese, with a pair of hands above each doing a careful test.
explanations.context: This card shows that the habits of careful practical work were written down in India, the Arab world and China long ago.

agreed.text: A good prediction, shared in time, is one of the strongest safety tools people have.
agreed.evidence: In October 2013 Cyclone Phailin was heading for the Odisha coast. The India Meteorological Department, with cyclone forecasting led by Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, said days ahead where and how hard it would strike. About a million people were moved inland before the storm arrived. Fewer than 50 people died. A cyclone of similar strength struck the same coast in 1999, with much poorer warning, and about 10,000 people died.

agreed.text: After people learn a result, they remember their earlier expectation as closer to the result than it was.
agreed.evidence: In 1975 the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff gave people accounts of events with different endings. People who were told an ending said that ending had been far more likely all along. They did not notice that knowing it had changed their view. The finding has been repeated many times.

agreed.text: A person needs about a fifth of a second to react to something seen, so hand timing cannot be trusted for very short events.
agreed.evidence: Reaction-time tests since the 1800s, and the simple test of catching a dropped ruler, give about 0.2 seconds for most people. That is why races decided by hundredths of a second are timed by light beams and cameras.

challenging.claim: Children are kept too safe. A childhood with no risk harms them more than scrapes and small burns would.
challenging.who: Ellen Sandseter and Leif Kennair, psychologists in Norway, in 2011, and Mariana Brussoni and colleagues in Canada, in 2015
challenging.for: Children who climb, use real tools and handle fire with care learn to judge danger for themselves. A review of studies in 2015 found that such play went with better health and with more active children. It found no clear sign of more serious injuries.
challenging.against: The studies are mostly of outdoor play in rich countries. They cannot say how much risk is the right amount. Some injuries, such as to an eye, do not heal, so many doctors and schools prefer to stay on the cautious side.
challenging.context: This view challenges the idea that the safest test is always the best one. It is here so that families think about what a child gains from handling a small, named risk.

challenging.claim: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water.
challenging.who: Erasto Mpemba, a schoolboy in Tanzania, in 1963. He published it with the physicist Denis Osborne in 1969. Aristotle wrote about something like it in his Meteorology, book 1, chapter 12, in the 4th century BCE.
challenging.for: Mpemba put a hot ice-cream mix in the freezer and saw it freeze before his classmates' cooler mixes. His classmates and his teacher laughed at him. He kept asking, and Osborne tested it and saw the same. In 2020 Avinash Kumar and John Bechhoefer in Canada showed a clear effect of this kind with a tiny glass bead cooling in water.
challenging.against: In 2016 Henry Burridge and Paul Linden in Britain repeated the water test with great care and found no such effect. They showed that where the thermometer sits in the cup can create a false one. Nobody has an agreed explanation for water.
challenging.context: This is a prediction almost everyone gets 'right' by common sense, that cold water freezes first, and yet careful people have reported the opposite. It shows why a result is judged by the test and not by who reports it.

challenging.claim: When ordinary people fear a risk more than experts do, the people are not simply mistaken. They are counting things that the experts' numbers leave out.
challenging.who: Paul Slovic, an American psychologist, in the journal Science in 1987
challenging.for: Experts usually count expected deaths in a year. Slovic found that other people also ask more questions. Is the risk chosen or forced on them? Is it understood? Could it harm many at once? Does it fall on children? These are real features of a risk.
challenging.against: Fears that ignore the numbers lead people to dread rare harms and overlook common ones, such as road accidents. Many safety scientists hold that spending should follow the count of lives saved.
challenging.context: This view questions who gets to decide what counts as risky. It matters at home too: a child's worry about a test deserves an answer, not only a number.

big_questions.q: A knife is a hazard in a drawer and in a hand, yet the risk is different. So where is the danger: in the knife, in the person, or somewhere between them?
big_questions.hint: Try changing only one of them at a time in your mind, and see if the danger changes.

big_questions.q: Your two hands disagreed about the same bowl of water, and the thermometer gave one number. Does that make the thermometer right and your hands wrong?
big_questions.hint: Ask what each of them was built to report, and what the number leaves out.

big_questions.q: You moved the cup away from the table's edge and nothing was spilled. How can you ever know if moving the cup was what kept you safe?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you would have to compare, and if you could ever see the thing that did not happen.

big_questions.q: If a prediction comes true, does that prove the reason behind it was right?
big_questions.hint: Think of someone who predicts rain because a crow cawed, and then the rain comes. Was the cawing the reason?

big_questions.q: Who should decide how much risk a test may have: the person doing it, the person hurt by it, or an expert with the numbers?
big_questions.hint: Think of a case where these are three different people, and what each one knows that the others do not.

big_questions.q: A snail, a plant or an ant cannot be asked if they agree to be in your test. Does that change what you may do?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you would want a being much bigger than you to decide about you.

big_questions.q: Marie Curie's work harmed her, and it also led to treatments that have saved many lives. Was the risk worth it, and who gets to say?
big_questions.hint: Notice that she did not know the risk, and ask if that changes your answer.

big_questions.q: If the world could be predicted perfectly, would your own choices be predicted too?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens if someone tells you their prediction of what you will do next.

big_questions.q: The sun has risen every day so far. Is that a good reason to predict that it will rise tomorrow, and can you say why without using the past again?
big_questions.hint: Try to give a reason, then check if your reason quietly assumes that the future will be like the past.

story.title: Two Forecasts on Pamban Shore
story.note: A made-up story. The people are imagined. What is real: on the coast of Ramanathapuram district in Tamil Nadu, near Pamban and Rameswaram, women dive for seaweed around the small islands of the Gulf of Mannar, wearing goggles and wrapping cloth round their fingers against sharp rock. The numbers in the story are invented for the story.
text: The boat was pulled half out of the water, and the sky over Pamban was still grey. Selvi, who was nine, sat on the edge of the boat with her school notebook. Her grandmother Muniyammal was winding strips of old sari cloth round each finger.
'Why the cloth, paatti?' asked Selvi, though she had asked before.

'Because the rock where the seaweed grows is sharp, and I need my fingers tomorrow also,' said Muniyammal. She held up her swimming goggles and looked at the strap. She pulled it twice and frowned. 'This one is tired.' She took a second pair from the bag. 'A diver with water in her eyes is a diver who cannot see the rock.'

Selvi's cousin Anthony, who was eleven, came down the sand with his phone held high. 'The weather office says wind from the north-east, 15 kilometres an hour now, 30 by two o'clock. Sea rough after two.'

Muniyammal did not look at the phone. She looked at the water for a long time. She watched how the waves folded over near the island, and which way the foam was dragged. 'The pull between the islands will turn before noon,' she said. 'When it turns, it runs hard out to the open side. We come up before that. The wind I do not know. It smells like any morning.'

'Two forecasts,' said Selvi. Her teacher had said that a prediction must be written before the test. She wrote on a clean page. Paatti: the current turns before 12. Phone: wind 30 by 2 o'clock. Paatti says nothing about the wind. The phone says nothing about the current.
Anthony laughed. 'You are marking paatti like an exam.'
'I am marking the phone also,' said Selvi.

Four women went out in the boat, and Selvi and Anthony went with them to mind the rope. At the island the divers slid into the water with their net bags. Selvi tied a coconut husk to a string and let the husk float beside the boat. For two hours the husk hung lazily on the island side.

At twenty minutes to twelve the string went tight. The husk swung round and pointed to the open sea. Selvi wrote: 11.40. She banged the side of the boat with the oar, three times, as she had been told. One by one the heads came up.
They were on the sand by half past twelve, with the bags only three-quarters full. Kaliammal, one of the divers, was not pleased. 'Another hour and my bag was full. The sea is like a plate.'

It was. At one o'clock the sea was a plate. At two o'clock Anthony held up a strip of cloth and counted how it flapped. 'This is not 30,' he said. 'This is nothing.' At three, the palm leaves began to hiss, and by four the waves were white all the way to the island.
Selvi marked her page. Paatti's current: predicted before 12, came at 11.40. Close. Phone's wind: predicted 2, came about 4. Two hours late, but it came.
'So paatti wins,' said Anthony.

'Paatti wins on the current,' said Selvi. 'She had nothing to say on the wind. The phone has never put its hand in this water. Paatti has, for forty years. The phone has watched the whole sky from far above, and she has not.' She chewed her pencil. 'Each one is good exactly where it has looked.'
Muniyammal was unwinding the cloth from her fingers. There was not one cut on them.
Kaliammal was still counting her loss. 'We came up at 11.40, and for four hours nothing happened. We could have stayed.'
'Could we?' said Muniyammal. 'You were on the open side. Did you feel the pull when you came up?'
Kaliammal said nothing for a moment. 'A little,' she said.

Selvi looked at her page. There was a line on it for what was predicted, and a line for what happened. There was no line for what would have happened if they had stayed. She did not know what to write there. Nobody did.
story.epiphany: A prediction is only as good as what its maker has watched. Selvi could mark the two forecasts because she wrote both down first and judged them by the sea, not by who made them. But she could not mark the safety. When a danger is avoided, the harm that did not happen leaves nothing to measure.
ask: Muniyammal's fingers had no cuts. Is that evidence that the cloth worked? What else would you need to know?
The phone was two hours late about the wind. Would you call that prediction accurate? What would your answer depend on?
Was coming up at 11.40 the right choice, even though nothing went wrong afterwards? How could anyone tell?

how_we_found_out.story: For most of history, people who were hurt at work were said to be unlucky or careless. Sickness from a trade was treated as part of the trade. It fitted what everyone saw: miners coughed, potters shook, and it had always been so. In the year 1700 an Italian doctor, Bernardino Ramazzini, published a book on the diseases of workers. He had gone into workshops and asked a question doctors did not ask: 'What is your work?' He matched each trade to its own illness. So the harm had causes, and causes can be changed. In 1910 the American doctor Alice Hamilton went from factory to factory in the state of Illinois, tracing lead poisoning. Owners told her that the workers were to blame for not washing. She showed that the lead dust in the air was to blame. In 1927 five radium dial painters took their employer to court. The case brought out that the company had known the danger, and in 1928 they won a settlement. Out of work like this came the modern rule that risks are named before work starts, and that the person in charge must reduce them.
how_we_found_out.who: Bernardino Ramazzini, Alice Hamilton, Grace Fryer and the radium dial painters, Harrison Martland
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Accidents and work sicknesses are bad luck or the worker's own carelessness, so nothing can be planned. It was believable because each injury looked like a separate event. Only when people counted the cases did they see that the same work gave the same harm again and again.

roots.context: You have chosen tools, named risks, written a prediction and checked it against the result. Now we ask what it means that a prediction can come true at all, and what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You wrote a number in your notebook before the sugar touched the warm water. Then the water gave a number of its own, and the two were close. You built your number from water you had watched earlier. So a pattern from the world was already at work in your thinking. Where your number missed, your thinking had not yet met that part of the world.
deep_truth.habit: We speak of 'my mind in here' and 'the world out there'. It sounds as if a prediction is made in one place and tested in another. That split makes a correct prediction look like a lucky match between two strangers.
deep_truth.evidence: In the dissolving test, your prediction for warm water came from your own results for cold water and room-warm water. Your reason in ink pointed at those two results. A prediction for something you had never watched at all would have been a blind guess.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who expects. Every step you take predicts that the floor will hold, and every sip predicts the taste. When a prediction of yours comes true, something of the world's pattern is living in you. So you are not looking in at the world through a window. You are a part of the world that has learned how other parts behave.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings act ahead of what is coming. A sunflower bud faces east before dawn, expecting the Sun. Some crows drop a nut on the road and wait for a wheel to crack it. A being who expects wrongly gets a surprise, and learns or suffers. Life can be seen as matter that has learned to expect, and to lower its own risks.
three.what_is_this_world: The world can be predicted in part. The tide keeps its table, and sugar keeps its habit in warm water. No one knows why the world has patterns that a mind can hold. The world also keeps surprises, such as tomorrow's cloud. A world with both pattern and surprise is one you can learn from and never finish learning.

roots.thread: A risk and a prediction are the same act looked at from two sides. Both are a mind running ahead of the present moment, using patterns it took in earlier. This can happen only if the one who knows and the thing known are made to the same pattern. Consciousness is the ground from which both arise, so a true prediction is that one ground recognising its own ways. Many scientists explain the match differently: brains were shaped over millions of years by the world they had to survive in. Both accounts agree on the plain fact you tested. You come to know by attending closely, and you come to know only what you have attended to.

teachings.teaching: Your right is to the work itself, and never to its fruits. Do not let the result be your reason for acting, and do not fall into doing nothing.
teachings.link: In practical work you control the choosing, the care and the doing. The result belongs to the world, and comes out as it comes. The verse and the notebook agree on one point: do the work fully, write the prediction honestly, and then accept the answer that arrives.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha told the Kalama people not to accept a teaching because it is repeated, or is in a scripture, or comes from a respected teacher. When you know for yourselves that a thing leads to harm, give it up. When you know for yourselves that it leads to good, take it up.
teachings.link: This is the rule Selvi follows in the story when she marks her grandmother and the phone in the same way. A prediction is judged by what happens and not by who made it. The sutta is about how to live, and the lesson borrows only its method.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 3, the story of Cook Ding, from China, about the 4th century BCE
teachings.teaching: Cook Ding has used one knife for nineteen years and its edge is still like new. He explains that he no longer hacks. He lets the blade follow the natural gaps in what he is cutting.
teachings.link: A tool used the right way works with the thing and not against it. Reading at eye level and starting at the ruler's zero are small cases of the same fit between a hand, a tool and the world.

science.text: Several brain scientists, among them Karl Friston and Anil Seth, propose that a brain's main work is predicting what the senses will report next. The brain then corrects itself when it is surprised. On this account, seeing and hearing are themselves predictions that are being checked.

Plants act ahead of events. Young sunflowers turn back to face east during the night, before the Sun rises. They keep doing so for a few days even under a lamp that does not move. Hagop Atamian and colleagues reported this in the journal Science in 2016.

other_view.who: The Charvaka thinkers of ancient India, as reported in Madhava's Sarvadarshanasangraha, chapter 1, of the 14th century CE, and the Scottish philosopher David Hume in 1748
other_view.view: Only what is directly seen is certain. A prediction rests on the belief that tomorrow will be like yesterday, and nothing can prove that belief without using it. So a match between prediction and result shows a habit of the mind that has worked so far. It does not show any deep fit between mind and world.

practice.title: One breath of prediction
practice.say: Sit comfortably and close your eyes. Before you breathe in, guess how many slow counts your next breath out will last. Hold the number in your mind. Now breathe in, and breathe out slowly while I count. Was your guess close? Do it twice more. Notice the small moment of waiting between the guess and the answer. Notice who made the guess, and who gave the answer.
practice.kid: Sit still and close your eyes. Guess how many slow counts your next breath out will last. Breathe in, then breathe out slowly and count. Was your guess close? Try it three times. Each time, notice the moment between your guess and your body's answer.

ask: Your body made the breath, and your mind made the guess about it. Are those two different makers, or one?
When your prediction is wrong, is the surprise in the world or in you?
A sunflower turns east before the Sun is up. Is the sunflower predicting? What would you look for to decide?
roots.art: A child with closed eyes and a number floating above her head, and beside her a young sunflower already facing a dark eastern horizon.

open_questions.q: Why can the world be predicted at all?
open_questions.why_open: Science finds patterns and uses them. It has no agreed account of why nature keeps to patterns that minds and mathematics can capture. In 1960 the physicist Eugene Wigner called this the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics. Some think the answer lies in how minds evolved, and some in the nature of mathematics. No test has yet decided it.

open_questions.q: Is the future already fixed by the present, or is some of it truly open?
open_questions.why_open: Chaos shows that we cannot predict some things in practice, which is a different matter from their being open. Quantum physics seems to show events without a deciding cause, but physicists still disagree about how to read it. No experiment so far settles the question.

open_questions.q: Does hot water ever really freeze faster than cold, and if so, why?
open_questions.why_open: Careful tests on water disagree with each other, and the effect, where reported, depends on the cup, the freezer and where the thermometer sits. An effect of this kind has been shown in other, simpler systems. For water there is no agreed result and no agreed explanation.
Measuring a risk is science. Deciding that a measured risk is acceptable is a judgement about what people value, and people value different things. No measurement can make that choice for them.

open_questions.q: Do all living beings predict, and is predicting the same thing in a plant, an ant and a person?
open_questions.why_open: Plants and many animals clearly act ahead of events. Scientists disagree on what to call this and on how it is done in beings with very different bodies. The idea that predicting is the main work of every brain is still a proposal being tested.

playtest: Not yet tried at a real table: every hands-on part (the dissolving test, the falling ruler, the three bowls, the tool-to-job activity, the coin drops, the kitchen risk hunt, the drying project, both challenges and the game) was written from known behaviour and has not been run with a family. Timings are estimates. The sugar test is the main risk: sugar types differ, so the stirring pace has a fix written in for sugar that is too fine or too coarse. Check that the cold, room-warm and warm times are far enough apart to see, and that the warm test stays under 45 degrees Celsius. terms.meaning: A test or an observation that you carry out yourself, with your own hands.
terms.example: Timing how long a wet cloth takes to dry on the line is practical work.
terms.art: A child hanging a wet cloth on a line beside a clock.

terms.meaning: The things you use to carry out a test or an observation.
terms.example: A steel tumbler, a spoon and a phone stopwatch are the equipment for timing sugar in water.
terms.art: A table with a tumbler, a spoon, a phone and a notebook laid out in a row.

terms.meaning: Something you can measure and give a number to.
terms.example: How tall a plant is, how long a cloth takes to dry and how warm the water is are all quantities.
terms.art: Three labelled arrows from a bean plant, a clock and a cup of water, each pointing to a number.

terms.meaning: How far it is from one end of something to the other. A ruler or a tape measures it.
terms.example: A bean plant that is 12 centimetres tall has a length of 12 centimetres.
terms.art: A ruler standing beside a small bean plant.

terms.meaning: How much space something takes up. For a liquid, a measuring cup measures it.
terms.example: A tumbler of water might hold 200 millilitres, and that is its volume.
terms.art: A measuring cup filled with water to the 200 mark.

terms.meaning: How much material a thing is made of. A weighing scale measures it, in grams or kilograms.
terms.example: One idli might have a mass of 40 grams on a kitchen scale.
terms.art: A kitchen scale with an idli on its plate and a number on the screen.

terms.meaning: How hot or cold something is. A thermometer measures it, in degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Cold water from the fridge is about 5 degrees Celsius, and warm tap water is about 40.
terms.art: A thermometer standing in a tumbler of warm water.

terms.meaning: A small unit of volume. There are 1,000 millilitres in one litre.
terms.example: A teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres of water.
terms.art: A teaspoon next to a one-litre bottle, with a label 'about 5 of these are 25'.

terms.meaning: The smallest amount a tool can show. A tool cannot tell apart amounts that are smaller than this.
terms.example: A kitchen jug marked every 100 millilitres cannot show 20 millilitres, but a medicine cup marked every 1 millilitre can.
terms.art: A jug with big marks beside a medicine cup with tiny marks.

terms.meaning: The mark on a tool where the counting starts. You line up what you measure with this mark.
terms.example: On many rulers the zero mark is a little way in from the end, so you line up the mark and not the edge.
terms.art: A ruler with an arrow pointing to its zero mark, set a little in from the end.

terms.meaning: Your eyes at the same height as the thing you are reading, so that you look straight across it.
terms.example: Bend down until your eye is level with the water line in the measuring cup before you read it.
terms.art: A child with her eye at the height of the water line in a measuring cup.

terms.meaning: The number a tool shows when you use it.
terms.example: The thermometer's reading in the warm water was 41 degrees.
terms.art: A thermometer with a pointer to 41.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures temperature. It needs about a minute in the water before its number stops changing.
terms.example: Stand the thermometer in the warm water and read it after a minute, not at once.
terms.art: A digital kitchen thermometer standing in a steel tumbler.

terms.meaning: A clock that you start and stop to measure how long something takes. A phone has one.
terms.example: Press start when the sugar touches the water, and press stop when the water is clear.
terms.art: A phone showing a stopwatch at 42.6 seconds.

terms.meaning: The body's sensors, such as those in the eyes, skin, ears, nose and tongue, that report what is around you. The body has many more kinds than the few best known.
terms.example: Your skin senses warm and cold, and your inner ear senses balance.
terms.art: A child's face and hands with arrows pointing to eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin.

terms.meaning: To put two things side by side and say how they are alike and different.
terms.example: Your two hands compare the middle bowl of water with the bowls they were in before.
terms.art: Two hands over three bowls of water, one hand over a cold bowl and one over a warm bowl.

terms.meaning: Anything that could cause harm.
terms.example: A kitchen knife is a hazard, whether it is in a drawer or in a hand.
terms.art: A closed drawer with a knife drawn faintly inside it.

terms.meaning: How likely a harm is, together with how bad it would be.
terms.example: A knife in a closed drawer has a tiny risk. A knife carried by a running child has a high risk.
terms.art: Two pictures of a knife, one in a drawer and one in a running child's hand.

terms.meaning: Hurt or damage to a person, another living being or a thing.
terms.example: A scald from hot water and a slip on a wet floor are two kinds of harm.
terms.art: A child holding a red hand beside a dripping tap.

terms.meaning: Something is likely if it will probably happen. It is unlikely if it will probably not.
terms.example: If you carry a full cup across a room while running, a spill is likely.
terms.art: A running child holding a full cup with drops flying out.

terms.meaning: A short list made before a test of what could cause harm, who could be harmed, and how likely and how bad the harm would be.
terms.example: Before the sugar test, you write: warm water could scald, a spill could cause a slip, a cup could break.
terms.art: A notebook page with three columns headed What could hurt, Who, and My plan.

terms.meaning: To take a hazard away completely, so that the test does not have it at all.
terms.example: If the test works with cold water, use cold water and the scald hazard is gone.
terms.art: A steaming pot crossed out beside a cup of cold water.

terms.meaning: To replace a hazard with a safer thing that does the same job.
terms.example: A plastic cup in place of a glass one is a swap.
terms.art: A glass cup crossed out and a plastic cup drawn beside it.

terms.meaning: Something put between people and a hazard, or distance kept from it, so that harm cannot easily reach them.
terms.example: A tray under the cups is a barrier, because a spill stays on the tray.
terms.art: A tray holding three cups on a table, with a spill staying inside its rim.

terms.meaning: Something you wear to guard your body from a hazard. It is the weakest kind of plan, because the hazard is still there.
terms.example: Tied-back hair and rolled-up sleeves keep loose things away from the work.
terms.art: A child with tied-back hair and rolled-up sleeves at a table.

terms.meaning: The order of ways to reduce a risk, from strongest to weakest: remove, swap, separate, and protect.
terms.example: Using cold water (remove) is stronger than using warm water with a grown-up pouring (separate).
terms.art: A ladder with four rungs labelled Remove, Swap, Separate and Protect from top to bottom.

terms.meaning: Liquid that runs out of its cup or bowl by mistake.
terms.example: A spill on a tiled floor makes it slippery.
terms.art: A tumbler lying on its side with water spreading across tiles.

terms.meaning: A burn from hot water or steam.
terms.example: Water that is too hot can scald skin, which is why we use warm tap water and never boiling water.
terms.art: A steaming kettle drawn beside a red warning mark on a hand.

terms.meaning: A tiny piece of matter, far too small to see. Everything solid, liquid and gas is built from atoms.
terms.example: A drop of water holds more atoms than anyone could count, and each is far smaller than a speck of dust.
terms.art: A water drop with a circle zooming in on a few tiny dots inside.

terms.meaning: A short written list of steps that must not be missed, read out and ticked at the moment of doing.
terms.example: Tray down, hair tied, cloth ready, grown-up near: tick each one before you start.
terms.art: A paper list with four ticks beside a tray and a cup.

terms.meaning: Giving out invisible rays that can harm the body. Some materials do this all the time, such as radium.
terms.example: Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive today.
terms.art: A lead-lined box on a library shelf with a notebook inside.

terms.meaning: A risk that people agree is small enough to take, because of what they gain. People do not all agree about how small that is.
terms.example: Most families accept the small risk of a cut when a grown-up slices an apple for a test.
terms.art: Two people on a see-saw, one holding a risk card and one holding a gain card.

terms.meaning: A step taken before something happens, to keep harm away.
terms.example: Putting a tray under the cups is a precaution against a spill.
terms.art: A hand sliding a tray under a row of cups.

terms.meaning: A plant, an animal, a fungus, a microbe or any other someone who is alive.
terms.example: A potted plant, a snail on the balcony and the ants on the wall are all living beings.
terms.art: A potted plant, a snail and a line of ants on a wall.

terms.meaning: A statement made before a test of what the result will be, with a reason for it.
terms.example: I predict the sugar will take 30 seconds in warm water, because cold took 70 and room-warm took 45.
terms.art: A notebook page that says 'I predict 30 seconds because...' with a pen beside it.

terms.meaning: What you already know that makes you expect a result.
terms.example: My reason is that warm water was faster than cold water in the first two tests.
terms.art: A thought bubble above a child's head that holds two small cups, a cold one and a warm one.

terms.meaning: A step of thinking from what you know to something you have not yet seen.
terms.example: Cold took longer than warm, so you infer that warm tap water will be even faster.
terms.art: A line of arrows from three known results to a question mark.

terms.meaning: Something you have seen or done many times.
terms.example: Sugar going into tea is a familiar sight.
terms.art: A cup of tea with a spoon, drawn in warm colours.

terms.meaning: Something you have not met before.
terms.example: Powdered jaggery in warm water is unfamiliar if you have never timed it.
terms.art: A small heap of rock salt crystals beside a question mark.

terms.meaning: A small solid piece with flat sides that meet in sharp corners, such as a grain of sugar or of rock salt.
terms.example: Look at a grain of sugar in torchlight. Its flat shiny sides are what make it a crystal.
terms.art: A close-up of sugar grains with flat shiny faces.

terms.meaning: To spread out into a liquid until the pieces are too small to see and the liquid is clear.
terms.example: Sugar dissolves in water, and the water turns clear again.
terms.art: Sugar crystals sinking into a cup of water, getting smaller in three steps.

terms.meaning: What you find out when you do the test.
terms.example: The result was 41 seconds for the sugar in warm water.
terms.art: A notebook page with a circled number under the heading Result.

terms.meaning: How far apart two numbers are. You find it by subtracting the smaller from the larger.
terms.example: You predicted 40 seconds and the result was 52 seconds, so the difference is 12 seconds.
terms.art: Two bars of different lengths with a bracket between their ends.

terms.meaning: How close a prediction or a measurement is to the true result.
terms.example: A prediction that is 2 seconds off a 50-second result is more accurate than one that is 12 seconds off.
terms.art: Two arrows hitting a target, one near the centre and one far from it.

terms.meaning: Looking back at something after you know how it ended. It makes people feel they expected the result all along.
terms.example: After a match, many people say 'I knew he would get out', though they never said it before.
terms.art: A cricket fan with a thought bubble that says 'I knew it' after the match.

terms.meaning: How far apart your repeated results are, found by taking the smallest from the largest.
terms.example: Runs of 48, 52 and 56 seconds have a spread of 8 seconds.
terms.art: Three dots on a number line from 48 to 56 with a bracket across them.

terms.meaning: The number in the middle when you line your results up from the smallest to the biggest.
terms.example: Runs of 56, 48 and 52 seconds line up as 48, 52, 56, so the middle value is 52 seconds.
terms.art: Three numbered cards in a row with the middle one raised.

terms.meaning: A result that comes out oddly because of luck, not because of the idea you are testing.
terms.example: One run of the sugar test took 20 seconds longer because your finger pressed stop late. Three runs show whether that was a fluke.
terms.art: A stopwatch with one number circled among three.

terms.meaning: A prediction about the future, such as tomorrow's weather, made from what is known now.
terms.example: The monsoon forecast says how much rain a year is likely to bring.
terms.art: A weather map of India with a cloud over the south-west coast.

terms.meaning: When something in the sky passes in front of another and blocks its light, as the Moon does to the Sun.
terms.example: Astronomers can predict a solar eclipse centuries ahead, to the minute.
terms.art: The Moon covering the Sun, with a thin ring of light round the edge.

terms.meaning: How far a prediction was from the result.
terms.example: A prediction of 40 seconds for a 52-second result is a miss of 12 seconds, too short.
terms.art: An arrow landing beside a target, with a bracket showing the gap.

terms.meaning: Something you take to be true without checking it.
terms.example: Assuming that both spoonfuls of sugar were the same size can hide the real reason for a miss.
terms.art: Two spoons that look the same, one heaped and one level.

terms.meaning: When tiny differences at the start grow into big differences later, so that nothing can be predicted far ahead even though the rules are fixed.
terms.example: A tiny change in a weather sum makes the forecast for ten days later completely different.
terms.art: Two paths that start almost together and end far apart.

terms.meaning: A very small piece of something, such as a grain of dust or an atom.
terms.example: A particle of sugar dissolving in water spreads out among the water.
terms.art: Tiny dots of sugar spreading through a cup of water in three steps.

terms.meaning: The part of physics that describes very small things, such as atoms and light. For some of them it can say only the chances of a result, and not which result will come.
terms.example: It can say that half of a set of radioactive atoms will break up in a certain time, but not which atom will go next.
terms.art: A handful of tiny dots with half of them faded, and a question mark over one dot.

terms.meaning: Whatever things are made of. Scientists have working meanings of matter that let them calculate, and no final answer to what matter finally is.
terms.example: A stone, water and air are all matter, and so are the cells of your body.
terms.art: A stone, a glass of water and a leaf drawn side by side.

games.title: The Safer Plan: a card game about making risks smaller
games.players: 2 to 4 players. A parent and a child are enough.
games.context: This is a card game in which every test card shows a hazard and every plan card shows a way to cut the risk. You score for the strongest kind of plan that really fits.
