setup.art: A table with 16 test cards in one pile and 20 plan cards in another, cut out from printed sheets.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 16 test cards and the 20 plan cards. Keep the two piles apart.

setup.art: Two players each holding four plan cards close to their chests, with the test pile and the plan pile between them.
setup.caption: 2. Deal 4 plan cards to each player.

setup.art: A test card face up in the middle and two plan cards face down beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn up a test card. Everyone puts one plan card face down.

printables.title: 16 test cards
items: Test: dissolve sugar in warm water. Hazard: warm water on a table.
Test: sprout moong seeds on a window sill. Hazard: small seeds near a toddler.
Test: make shadows with a lamp. Hazard: a hot bulb that can burn fingers.
Test: dry a wet shirt in the sun. Hazard: leaning over a balcony rail to hang it.
Test: float and sink things in a steel basin. Hazard: water on the floor.
Test: watch ants carry sugar. Hazard: you could crush or trap the ants.
Test: smell different spices to compare. Hazard: sniffing chilli powder up close.
Test: stir salt into water to see how much dissolves. Hazard: tasting the water by mistake.
Test: roll a marble down a ramp. Hazard: a marble on the floor can make someone slip.
Test: time ice melting in two cups. Hazard: a glass cup that could crack.
Test: mark your height on the door each month. Hazard: stretching on tiptoe on a wet floor.
Test: try a magnet on steel things. Hazard: a small magnet a toddler could swallow.
Test: fly paper planes in a corridor. Hazard: a plane hitting someone's eye.
Test: find which cloth soaks up most water. Hazard: a wet floor after wringing.
Test: watch the Sun's shadow of a stick for an hour. Hazard: looking at the Sun to find it.
Test: warm milk to set curd. Hazard: a pan of hot milk.

items.f: Use cold water. The test works without any warming.
items.b: REMOVE. Taking the hazard away leaves nothing to go wrong. It fits tests that do not need warmth.

items.f: Skip the taste. Look and smell from a distance.
items.b: REMOVE. Nothing is swallowed, so poison from a food or powder cannot happen.

items.f: Work at ground level. Nobody has to climb or lean.
items.b: REMOVE. Without a climb, a fall from a height cannot happen.

items.f: Watch the animal where they already are. Do not catch or move them.
items.b: REMOVE. Not catching removes the harm of trapping, and the animal stays free.

items.f: Use daylight from a window. Switch off the lamp.
items.b: REMOVE. With no lamp, there is no hot bulb and no mains wire to touch.

items.f: Use a plastic cup in place of a glass one.
items.b: SWAP. A plastic cup does the same job and cannot cut. It is safer than glass but stronger plans exist.

items.f: Use big objects, too big to swallow, in place of tiny ones.
items.b: SWAP. A big object does the job of a small one without the swallowing hazard.

items.f: Use a cool torch in place of a lamp or a flame.
items.b: SWAP. A torch gives light and leaves out the hot bulb or the flame.

items.f: Use warm tap water in place of boiling water.
items.b: SWAP. A safer thing replaces a risky one and the test still works.

items.f: Use a sealed bottle in place of an open bowl.
items.b: SWAP. A closed lid stops water slopping, though the bottle can still be dropped.

items.f: Work on a tray, so spills stay on the tray.
items.b: SEPARATE. A rim is a barrier between the water and the floor. It does not stop the spill, only where it goes.

items.f: A grown-up does the risky step while you stand back.
items.b: SEPARATE. Distance puts the child out of the way of the hazard, though the hazard stays.

items.f: Keep babies and pets in another room.
items.b: SEPARATE. A closed door is a barrier between small hands and the work.

items.f: Put a mat under the work, so nothing is slippery.
items.b: SEPARATE. A mat is a barrier between the water and the floor, but the water is still there.

items.f: Stand a long step back from anyone throwing or swinging.
items.b: SEPARATE. Distance keeps the swing away from other people.

items.f: Tie back long hair and roll up loose sleeves.
items.b: PROTECT. This guards your body, but the hazard is still there, so it is the weakest plan.

items.f: Wear chappals or shoes with grip.
items.b: PROTECT. A better grip helps you stay up on a wet floor, but the wet floor remains.

items.f: Wear a cap and keep to the shade.
items.b: PROTECT. A cap guards your head from the Sun, but the Sun is still there.

items.f: Wear a plastic apron.
items.b: PROTECT. The apron guards clothes and skin, and the hazard is still there.

items.f: Wear glasses or goggles to guard your eyes.
items.b: PROTECT. Goggles can slip, and the hazard is still in front of you.

printables.title: Score sheet, to copy by hand: a row for each of 8 rounds and a column for each player
items: Round 1 to Round 8. Write the points each player won.

rules: Each plan card has a kind on its back. Remove is worth 4 points, Swap 3, Separate 2 and Protect 1. Keep the backs hidden until the reveal.
Deal 4 plan cards to each player. Put the rest face down as the plan pile. Shuffle the test cards and put them face down.
In each round, turn up one test card. Every player puts one plan card from their hand face down.
Turn all the plan cards over. Each player says in one sentence how their plan makes the risk smaller for this test.
The other players decide if each plan really fits this test. A plan that does not fit scores 0 and goes to the discard pile. With two players, the other player decides.
Among the plans that fit, the highest kind scores its points. If two plans are of the same kind and both fit, both score.
Everyone draws back up to 4 plan cards. If the plan pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile and carry on.
Play 8 rounds. The player with the most points wins. Players who tie share the win.
Two plans of a different kind can both be worth defending, so say why aloud. A Remove card that does not fit loses to a Protect card that does.

flow.do: Cut out the 16 test cards and the 20 plan cards. Keep them in two piles. Read three plan cards together and say which kind each one is.
flow.say: Each plan card is one of four kinds. Remove takes the hazard away. Swap replaces it with a safer thing. Separate puts a barrier or distance in the way. Protect only guards your body. Which is strongest, do you think?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read three plan cards. Guess their kind.
flow.parent: Cutting is for a grown-up if the child is under 8. Do not read the card backs aloud during play. Keep the cards in an envelope for next time.

flow.do: Play round 1 and round 2. Turn up a test card, and everyone puts down a plan card. Turn them over, say why each fits and score.
flow.say: Here is the test and its hazard. Which of your plans cuts the risk most? Do not show me yet. Now turn them over. Why does yours fit?
flow.kid: Turn up a test card. Put down a plan card. Say why it fits.

ask.q: Which of the four kinds is strongest, and why is it not always the best choice?
good: Remove is strongest, but it may not fit the test, because a test that needs warmth cannot remove warmth.

flow.do: Play the other 6 rounds. Add up the points. Share the winner's best plan.
flow.say: Add your points. Whose plan was the strongest kind and also really fitted? Which test card was hardest to make safe?
flow.kid: Finish the rounds. Add up the points.
flow.parent: No test has zero risk. If someone says a plan 'makes it totally safe', ask what could still go wrong.

experiments.title: The dissolving-time test: choose your tools, name the risks, predict, then judge your prediction
experiments.context: In this test you time sugar dissolving in cold, room-warm and warm water. You predict the warm time from the first two, and then check how close you came.
experiments.question: How long does a level teaspoon of sugar take to dissolve in cold, room-warm and warm water? Can you predict the warm time from the first two?
experiments.predict: Before the warm test, use your cold and room-warm times to write a number for warm water. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: These stay the same. The cup is filled to the same line. The sugar comes from the same bag, one level teaspoon each time. The spoon, the stirring and the stop signal do not change. The same person starts and stops the clock. Only the warmth of the water changes. Cold and room-warm are each run twice and warm is run three times, because a finger on a stopwatch is never exactly on time. In the second round, only the solid changes.
results_table: Temperature in degrees Celsius, if you have a thermometer
experiments.safety: Use warm tap water only, never boiling water, and let a grown-up pour it. Stand the cups on a tray. Use plastic and not glass. Do not taste anything in the test.
experiments.record: Fill the table for cold, room-warm and warm water. Write your prediction and its reason before the warm test. After it, write the middle value, the spread and the miss. Then write one sentence each for what you thought, what you saw and why. Do the same for rock salt or jaggery.

materials.item: clear plastic cups of about 200 millilitres
granulated sugar, about 2 tablespoons in a small bowl
a teaspoon, and a stiff card or ruler edge to level it
a steel spoon for stirring, the same one every time
a measuring cup or a jug with a mark at about 100 millilitres, or a pen line on each cup
a phone with a stopwatch
a kitchen thermometer, if you have one (digital, not glass)
a tray
a dark cloth or dark plate to put under the cup
a spill cloth
water from the fridge, water that has stood out for an hour, and warm tap water
a teaspoon of crushed rock salt or powdered jaggery
paper, a pen with ink and a notebook

setup.art: A table with a measuring cup, a one-litre jug, a ruler, a phone stopwatch, a wall clock and a thermometer, and a child's hand picking up the stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Choose the tools. Pick one for how much, one for how long and one for how warm.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns headed What could hurt, Who could be hurt and My plan, and a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Write the risks of the test and a plan for each one.

setup.art: A tray on a table holding a dark cloth, a clear plastic cup of water, a level teaspoon of sugar and a spoon, with a spill cloth beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Set the tray. Fill the cup to the line. Add one level teaspoon of sugar.

setup.art: A cup of water seen from the side, with a few sugar crystals at the bottom in the first picture and clear water in the second, and a phone stopwatch beside each.
setup.caption: 4. Start the clock when the sugar touches the water. Stop it when the water is clear.

setup.art: A folded paper slip under a tray, and a results table with three columns for cold, room-warm and warm water.
setup.caption: 5. Write your prediction in ink and fold it away before the warm test.

flow.do: Put these on the table: a measuring cup, a one-litre jug, a ruler, a phone with a stopwatch and a wall clock. Add a thermometer if you have one. Ask your child to pick one tool for each question: how much water, how long, and how warm.
flow.say: We will time sugar in water. We need to know three things. How much water? How long does the sugar take? How warm is the water? Which tool answers each one, and why that one?
flow.kid: Look at the tools. Pick one for each question. Say why you chose it.

ask.q: Which tool will you use to time the sugar, and why not the wall clock?
good: The phone stopwatch, because it shows seconds, and the wall clock has no seconds hand.

flow.parent: Good picks are the measuring cup for the water, the phone stopwatch for the time and the thermometer for the warmth. The wall clock has no seconds hand, so it cannot show 20 seconds. A ruler measures length, which this test does not need. If you have no thermometer, skip the numbers and call the waters cold, room and warm. Never use a glass thermometer that holds mercury.

flow.do: Walk through the whole test in your head, from setting up to cleaning up. In a notebook, write three columns: What could hurt, Who could be hurt, and My plan. Fill in a row for each risk you find.
flow.say: Before we start, let us ask what could go wrong. Take each step in turn. What could hurt someone? Who could it hurt? How likely is it? Then we write one plan for each.
flow.kid: Think through each step. Write what could hurt, who, and your plan.
flow.parent: Let your child name as many risks as they can. Then add the ones they miss. Warm water could scald, so we use warm tap water and never boiling water, and a grown-up pours it. A spill could make the floor slippery, so the cups stand on a tray and a cloth is ready. A glass cup could crack, so use plastic. Nothing here is meant to be eaten, so nobody tastes anything. A small child or a pet could knock things over, so keep them in another room. Sugar water draws ants, so wipe up at the end.

check.q: Which plan cuts the scald risk the most?
options: A grown-up pours the water slowly
Use warm tap water and never boiling water
check.why: Swapping boiling water for warm tap water makes the hazard itself smaller. Pouring slowly only helps while nothing goes wrong, and an apron guards your clothes but leaves the hazard there.

flow.do: Set a tray in the middle of the table and tie back long hair. Put a dark cloth on the tray and a clear cup on the cloth. Keep a spill cloth beside you. Read this checklist aloud and tick each line: tray down, hair tied, cloth ready, grown-up near, prediction paper ready. Fill a teaspoon with sugar and slide a stiff card across the top to level it. Then do one practice run with cold water, and do not write the time down.
flow.say: Everything has its place. Now one practice run. Pour water to the line and add one level spoon of sugar. Start the clock as the sugar touches the water. Stir one slow circle each second, and say the count aloud.
flow.kid: Set the tray and cup. Do one practice run. Stir one circle each second.
flow.parent: The edge of a ruler works as well as a card for levelling. The run ends when no crystals show on the dark cloth or in the water, and the water looks clear. If the practice run is still cloudy after 2 minutes, pour it away and stir two circles each second in every cup from now on. If it clears in under 10 seconds, your sugar is very fine, so stir one circle every two seconds in every cup. Keep your chosen stirring the same for the whole test.

flow.do: Fill the cup to the line with cold water from the fridge bottle. Add one level teaspoon of sugar, start the clock and stir one circle each second. Stop the clock when the water is clear, and write the time. Do two runs with cold water and two with room-warm water from a jug that has stood out for an hour. Read each jug's temperature after a minute.
flow.say: Before the first run, which water do you think will be faster, cold or room-warm? Why do you think so? Now measure and see.
flow.kid: Do two cold runs and two room-warm runs. Write each time.

ask.q: Which water do you think will be faster, cold or room-warm, and why?
good: Room-warm, because sugar vanishes faster in warm tea than in cold juice.

flow.parent: Use fresh water and the same spoon each time, and rinse the cup between runs. Do not tell your child the answer. If two runs of the same water differ by a few seconds, that is normal. A finger on a stopwatch is never exactly on time. In winter the room water may be nearly as cold as the fridge water. Write the real numbers whatever they are.

flow.do: Cover the results table. On a slip of paper, write: Warm tap water. I predict ___ seconds, because ___. Write in ink. Fold the slip and put it under the tray.
flow.say: Warm tap water is warmer than both of your cups. What time do you expect? Use your cold and room-warm times. Write the number and your reason in ink.
flow.kid: Look at your two times. Write a number for warm water. Write your reason.

ask.q: What number did you write, and what in your results made you choose it?
good: A number lower than the room-warm time, with a reason taken from the first two results.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A good reason uses the data. For example: 'Cold took 70 seconds and room-warm took 45. Warmer water should save about 25 more, so about 20.' Any honest number with a reason is fine. The ink matters. A number that can be changed after the result cannot be judged.

flow.do: A grown-up fills a jug with warm tap water. Check it with the inside of a wrist or a thermometer. It must feel comfortably warm and read under 45 degrees Celsius. The grown-up pours one cup to the line. Time three runs, with fresh warm water for each run, and write each time.
flow.say: I will pour. You press start when the sugar touches the water. Same spoon, same stirring, same stop signal. We do three runs, because one run can be a fluke.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the warm water. You do the timing. Do three runs.
flow.parent: The child never carries or pours the warm water. If your tap gives hot water, add cold water until it feels comfortably warm on the inside of your wrist. Warm water cools a little between runs, so use fresh water each time. Whatever numbers you get are the real result. If warm water clears in under 10 seconds, the finger on the stopwatch matters more, so say so in the table.

flow.do: Open the slip. Find the middle value of the three warm runs. Find the spread, which is the biggest time minus the smallest. Subtract your prediction from the middle value to get the miss. Write which way you missed, too short or too long.
flow.say: Your three runs differ from each other by this much. That wobble is the spread. Is your miss smaller than the wobble? If so, this test cannot tell your prediction from the truth.
flow.kid: Find the middle time and the spread. Find how far off you were.

ask.q: Was your miss bigger or smaller than the spread? What does that tell you?
good: If smaller, the prediction was as close as the test can judge. If bigger, the doing, the tool or the reason needs another look.

flow.parent: If the miss is inside the spread, the prediction is as accurate as this test can show. If it is outside, it is a real miss. Then ask three questions in this order. Did we do every run the same way? Was the tool the same each time? Is the reason about warmth missing something? A test like this cannot say why the numbers fall as they do. Ask your child what else they would test.
flow.think: If a friend did this test with the same sugar, would they get the same numbers? What would make them differ?

flow.do: Choose rock salt or powdered jaggery, whichever you have. On a new slip, predict in ink how long one level teaspoon takes in warm water, and why. A grown-up pours warm water, and you time two runs. Stop at 3 minutes if the water is not clear.
flow.say: This one is new. Sugar and rock salt are alike in one way and different in another. What do you think will stay the same, and what will change? Write your number and your reason first.
flow.kid: Write your guess and your reason. Time two runs. Stop at 3 minutes.
flow.parent: Good reasons: both dissolve in water, so warmth should still help. Rock salt crystals are bigger, so it may be slower than sugar. Powdered jaggery has tiny grains, so it may be about as fast as sugar. Jaggery water stays brown, so stop when no grains show on the dark cloth. If the water is still cloudy at 3 minutes, write 'more than 180 seconds'. A prediction of 'slower than sugar' is then right about the direction. Pour the water down the sink, rinse the cups and wipe the table, because sugar water draws ants.

experiments.title: The falling ruler: how late is your finger on a stopwatch?
experiments.context: In this test a ruler is dropped and you catch it, and the distance it falls tells you how long you took to react. You find out why timing a short event by hand is never exact.
experiments.question: How far does a ruler fall before you catch it, and what does that tell us about how late a finger on a stopwatch is?
experiments.predict: Before you drop the first ruler, guess how many centimetres it will fall before you catch it. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: These stay the same: the ruler, the partner, the start position of your fingers and the eyes-on-zero rule. The partner lets go at a different time every drop, so that you cannot guess. For the second hand, only the hand changes. Ten drops are done for each hand, because one catch can be a fluke.
experiments.record: Write ten numbers for each hand. Circle the middle value for each. Find the spread for each hand. Then write one sentence each for what you thought, what you saw and why.

materials.item: a 30 centimetre ruler, plastic, wood or steel, with the zero at the end
a partner, such as a parent or a friend
paper, a pencil and a results table of ten rows for each hand

setup.art: A child with finger and thumb open around the zero end of a hanging ruler, and a partner's hand holding the top.
setup.caption: 1. A partner holds the ruler. Your fingers are open around the zero mark.

setup.art: The ruler falling, with a blur, and the child's fingers closing on it.
setup.caption: 2. The partner lets go without warning. You close your fingers as fast as you can.

setup.art: A hand reading the ruler number at the top of a thumb, and a results table with ten rows.
setup.caption: 3. Read the number at the top of your thumb and write it in the table.

flow.do: Ask a partner to hold a 30 centimetre ruler by its top end, with the zero end hanging down. Put your thumb and first finger around the zero mark, not touching the ruler. Look at the zero mark, not at your partner's hand.
flow.say: A ruler will drop when you least expect it. You must close your fingers as fast as you can. Before we start, how many centimetres do you think it will fall before you catch it, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hold your fingers round the zero mark. Guess how far the ruler will fall.

ask.q: How far do you think the ruler will fall, and why?
good: A small number such as 5 centimetres, with a reason such as 'my hand is fast'.

flow.parent: Write the guess down. Most children guess 2 to 5 centimetres. Do not say the real answer. Without a partner, ask any grown-up or friend to drop the ruler.

flow.do: Practise three drops without writing anything. The partner lets go at a different moment each time, anywhere between 2 and 5 seconds after saying 'ready'. Do not count aloud.
flow.say: I will say 'ready', wait a little, and then let go. Close your fingers as soon as you see it move.
flow.kid: Do three practice drops. Watch the zero mark.
flow.parent: A random wait stops your child from guessing the moment. If the ruler falls right through, check that eyes are on the zero mark and fingers are open about 3 centimetres wide.

flow.do: Do ten real drops with the same hand. After each one, read the number on the ruler at the top of your thumb. Write it in the table. Slide the ruler back into place each time.
flow.say: Ten drops, ten numbers. Write each one. Some will be bigger and some smaller. That is normal.
flow.kid: Do ten drops. Write each number.
flow.parent: Typical numbers are between 12 and 22 centimetres. If a drop goes past 30 centimetres, do it again, because the child was probably looking away.

flow.do: Now swap hands. First write a guess for the other hand, and a reason. Then do ten drops with that hand and write the numbers.
flow.say: Will the other hand catch higher or lower, or about the same? Write your guess and your reason first. Then try it.
flow.kid: Guess which hand is faster, and why. Try ten drops.

ask.q: Which hand do you think is faster, and why?
good: Either answer is fine, with a reason. The test will show whether any difference is bigger than the spread.

flow.parent: Most children find the two hands differ by only a few centimetres, which is often smaller than the spread within one hand. If it is, the test cannot tell the hands apart.

flow.do: Use the table to turn each number into a time. Here is the table. 5 centimetres is 0.10 seconds. 10 is 0.14 and 15 is 0.18. 20 is 0.20. 25 is 0.23 and 30 is 0.25. Find the middle number for each hand and its time. Find the spread for each hand.
flow.say: Your hand took about this many tenths of a second to answer your eyes. A stopwatch press has the same delay.
flow.kid: Look up your middle number in the table. Write the time.
flow.parent: The times come from the physics of falling things, and they are rounded. You do not need the sum, only the table.

flow.do: Think of timing a toy car that rolls for 3 seconds by hand. Say how much of the time a delay of 0.2 seconds is. Then think of a snap that lasts 0.3 seconds.
flow.say: A finger is about a fifth of a second late. For a long event, that is small. For a very short one, it is most of the time. So when should you trust a hand-timed number?
flow.kid: A finger is 0.2 seconds late. When does that matter?

ask.q: When can you trust a hand-timed number, and when not?
good: For long events a fifth of a second is small. For very short events it is most of the result, so use a camera or a longer distance.

flow.parent: 0.2 out of 3 is about one in fifteen. 0.2 out of 0.3 is two thirds. Races decided by hundredths of a second use light beams and cameras for this reason.

experiments.safety: Use a plastic or wooden ruler, not a metal one with sharp edges. The partner lets the ruler fall straight down and never swings or flicks it. Keep faces well away from the ruler.

activities.title: Three bowls of water for two hands
activities.context: In this activity you put your two hands into the same bowl of water and find that they disagree. You see why a thermometer is useful and why your skin is still worth listening to.
activities.safety: Use warm tap water only, never hot water. A grown-up pours it and checks it on the inside of a wrist first.
activities.record: Write what the left hand said and what the right hand said. Write the thermometer number if you have one.

materials.item: steel or plastic bowls
cold water, with ice cubes in summer, and warm tap water
a kitchen thermometer, if you have one
a tray and a towel

setup.art: Three bowls in a row on a tray, labelled cold, in between and warm, with steam from the right-hand one.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three bowls: cold, in between and warm.

setup.art: A child with a left hand in the cold bowl and a right hand in the warm bowl, and a clock showing one minute.
setup.caption: 2. Keep your hands in the outer bowls for one minute.

setup.art: A child with both hands in the middle bowl, looking puzzled, and a thermometer standing in the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Put both hands in the middle bowl, then read the thermometer.

flow.do: Set three bowls in a row on a tray. A grown-up fills the left bowl with cold water. The right bowl gets warm tap water that feels comfortable on the inside of a wrist. The middle bowl gets half cold and half warm.
flow.say: We will use three bowls of water. One is cold, one is warm and one is in between. Do not touch them yet. What do you think will happen to your hands?
flow.kid: Look at the three bowls. A grown-up fills them.
flow.parent: Cold bowl: cold tap water, with four ice cubes in summer. Warm bowl: warm tap water, comfortable on the inside of your wrist and under 45 degrees Celsius. Middle bowl: one cup from each, with no ice cubes. If your tap is only slightly warm in the hot months, the test still works, because the cold bowl is much colder than the middle one.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess what each hand will say about the middle bowl. Then put the left hand in the cold bowl and the right hand in the warm bowl. Keep them there for one minute.
flow.say: Left hand in the cold bowl, right hand in the warm bowl. Wait for one minute. Before you move them, guess what each hand will feel when it goes into the middle bowl. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put one hand in each outer bowl. Wait one minute. Make a guess.

ask.q: What do you think each hand will feel in the middle bowl, and why?
good: Any guess with a reason is fine. Many children think both hands will feel the same.

flow.do: Put both hands into the middle bowl at the same time. Ask what each hand says. Write down what the left hand says and what the right hand says.
flow.say: Both hands into the middle bowl, now. What does the left hand say? What does the right hand say? Is it the same water?
flow.kid: Put both hands in the middle bowl. What does each hand say?
flow.parent: The left hand, which came from cold, feels warm. The right hand, which came from warm, feels cool. The same water feels different to each.

flow.do: Stand a thermometer in the middle bowl and read it after one minute at eye level. Ask whose report your child trusts, and what they would use to check a baby's bath.
flow.say: The thermometer gives one number for the middle bowl. Your hands gave two answers. Is either hand wrong? What would you use to check that a baby's bath is safe?
flow.kid: Read the thermometer. Compare it with what your hands said.

ask.q: Which would you trust to check a baby's bath, and why?
good: A thermometer, because it gives one number that does not depend on where it just was.

flow.parent: Skin reports a change from where it just was. A thermometer reports against a fixed scale. Neither is wrong. Tools give numbers, and senses notice what is worth measuring. If you have no thermometer, a grown-up's wrist is a third opinion.
flow.think: Your hands compare. What else in your day is judged by comparing and not by a number?

activities.title: Match the tool to the job
activities.context: In this activity you meet three small jobs and choose a tool for each one. You see why a tool must fit the size of the thing, and what to do when no tool is fine enough.
activities.record: Fill a table with the job, the quantity, the tool you chose, its smallest mark and why another tool would not fit.

materials.item: a 30 centimetre ruler
a one-litre jug marked every 100 millilitres
a medicine cup marked in millilitres, or a teaspoon
a phone with a stopwatch
a plastic bottle cap
10 grains of rice
a marble, a small ball or a round pencil, and a hardback book for a ramp
a wall clock with no seconds hand

setup.art: A table with a ruler, a jug, a medicine cup, a stopwatch and a bottle cap, with a hand picking the medicine cup.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the tools and pick one for each job.

setup.art: Ten grains of rice lined up end to end along a ruler beside a single grain.
setup.caption: 2. Measure one grain. Then measure ten in a row and divide by ten.

setup.art: A marble at the top of a book ramp, a phone stopwatch and a wall clock with no seconds hand.
setup.caption: 3. Time the roll with the phone and with the wall clock.

flow.do: Set out a ruler, a one-litre jug marked every 100 millilitres, and a medicine cup or a teaspoon. Add a phone stopwatch and a bottle cap. Job one is to find how much water one bottle cap holds. Ask your child to pick a tool.
flow.say: How much water fits in this bottle cap? Which tool will you pick? What is the smallest mark on each one? Which tool can show an amount as small as this?
flow.kid: Pick a tool to measure the water in a cap. Check its smallest mark.

ask.q: Why can the jug not measure the water in one cap?
good: Its smallest mark is 100 millilitres, which is far bigger than the water in a cap.

flow.parent: The jug cannot show it, because its smallest mark is far bigger than the cap's water. If your cup shows 1 millilitre marks, fill the cap to the brim ten times into the cup and read the total. Divide by 10. With only a teaspoon, count how many capfuls fill it. A teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres, so a teaspoon that takes 3 capfuls means a cap holds about 1.7 millilitres. Most caps hold between 1 and 3 millilitres.

flow.do: Job two is the length of one grain of rice. Lay ten grains in a row, touching end to end, along the ruler. Read the whole length and divide by ten. Then measure one grain alone and compare.
flow.say: How long is one grain of rice? Measure one grain, then measure ten in a line and divide by ten. Which gives you the more careful answer? Why?
flow.kid: Measure one grain. Then measure ten in a row and divide by ten.
flow.parent: A grain is about 6 to 9 millimetres. One grain alone is read to the nearest millimetre, which is a big share of its length. Ten grains in a row spread that small error over ten grains. Line up the first grain at the zero mark, not the end of the ruler.

flow.do: Job three is the time a marble or small ball takes to roll along a book ramp. Time it with the phone stopwatch. Then try the wall clock with no seconds hand. Say which tool fits the job and why.
flow.say: How long does the ball take to roll down? Time it with the phone, then try to time it with the wall clock. What happens? Which tool fits?
flow.kid: Time the roll with the phone. Try the wall clock too.
flow.parent: The roll takes about 1 to 2 seconds. A clock with no seconds hand cannot show a time this short. The phone shows tenths and hundredths of a second, though your finger is about 0.2 seconds late. Run it three times.

flow.do: Fill a table with four columns: the job, the quantity, the tool you chose and the smallest mark of that tool. Add a fifth column for a tool that would not fit, and why.
flow.say: For each job, which quantity were you finding out? Which tool fitted, and which did not? Would you use this ruler to measure our room? Why not?
flow.kid: Fill the table. Write why each unfit tool would not do.
flow.parent: Do not rank tools as good or bad. A tool fits when its smallest mark is much smaller than your amount and it is not so fine that you must repeat it many times. A 15 centimetre ruler could measure a room, but you would lay it down about 40 times and each laying adds a small mistake.
flow.think: What job could you do today with no tool at all, only your senses? When would a tool do better?

activities.safety: Rice grains and bottle caps are small enough for a toddler to swallow. Keep them away from babies and small children, and put them away when you finish. Wipe up any water at once.

activities.title: How many drops fit on a coin? Predict, test and judge
activities.context: In this activity you predict how many drops of water a coin can hold, test it three times and compare your miss with the spread. Then you predict for a second coin, which is new to you.
activities.record: Write each guess and its reason. Write three counts for each coin. Find the middle count and the spread. Write whether each guess was inside or outside the spread.

materials.item: a small coin and a larger coin, both flat and clean
a plastic dropper, or a drinking straw
a small cup of water
a tray and a dry cloth
paper and a pencil

setup.art: A small coin on a dry tray with a plastic dropper above it, and a cup of water beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a clean, dry coin flat on a tray.

setup.art: Drops sitting in a dome on the coin, with one drop about to fall from the dropper.
setup.caption: 2. Add drops one at a time and count until the water spills.

setup.art: A small and a large coin side by side, with a results table of three runs for each.
setup.caption: 3. Predict and test the bigger coin, then judge your two predictions.

flow.do: Wipe the small coin dry and lay it flat on a dry tray. Fill the cup with water. Ask your child to write how many drops will fit before the water spills over, and why.
flow.say: How many drops of water can sit on this coin before it spills over? Write your number and why you think so, before we try.
flow.kid: Write how many drops you think will fit. Write why.
flow.parent: Most families see between 10 and 40 drops on a small coin, so any guess is fine. A clean, dry coin is the key. A greasy coin makes the drops flatten and spill sooner. Wipe it with a dry cloth each time.

flow.do: Hold the dropper or straw just above the coin. Add drops one at a time and count aloud until the water spills over the edge. Dry the coin. Do this three times and write each count.
flow.say: Drop, count, drop, count. Stop when the water runs over the edge. Do it three times. Are the counts the same?
flow.kid: Add drops one at a time. Count until it spills. Do three runs.
flow.parent: To use a straw as a dropper, dip it in the water, put a finger over the top end and lift. Then ease your finger off to let drops fall. Keep the same height above the coin every time. The three counts will differ by a few drops. That is the spread.

flow.do: Lay the bigger coin on the tray. Ask your child to predict its count from the small coin's result, with a reason. Then do three runs the same way and write each count.
flow.say: This coin is wider. How many drops do you think it will hold? Use what you found out with the small coin. Write your number and your reason first.
flow.kid: Guess for the bigger coin. Then do three runs.

ask.q: What number did you write for the bigger coin, and why?
good: A larger number than the small coin's, with a reason about the bigger top.

flow.parent: A wider coin has a bigger top and holds more, though not in exact proportion. A good reason says that a bigger flat top has room for more water.

flow.do: Find the middle count and the spread for each coin. Compare each miss with the spread. Say which prediction was closer, and whether you missed by more than the wobble of your own counts.
flow.say: Was your guess inside the spread or outside it? Which guess was closer, the first or the second? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find the middle and the spread for each coin. Judge your two guesses.
flow.parent: You may find the second guess was closer, because the child had data to build on. Do not push this. Let the numbers say it.
flow.think: Would a drop that is twice as big change your counts? Which tool would you change to get a fairer count?

activities.safety: Coins are small enough for a toddler to swallow, so keep them away from babies and small children. Wipe up spilled water at once so nobody slips.

activities.title: A risk hunt in your own kitchen
activities.context: In this activity you walk through your kitchen with a grown-up and name five hazards. You then judge the risk of each today and plan a safer way using the four kinds of plan.
activities.safety: A grown-up stays beside the child. Nothing in the kitchen is touched or used.
activities.record: Write five hazards, the risk of each today and a plan for the riskiest, with its kind.

materials.item: five small cards or slips of paper
a pencil

setup.art: A child with a grown-up in a kitchen, pointing to a high shelf with a glass jar.
setup.caption: 1. Walk through the kitchen and name five hazards.

setup.art: Five cards laid in a row, each with a hazard and a mark for low, medium or high risk.
setup.caption: 2. Rate the risk of each hazard today.

setup.art: A card turned over with a drawing of a plan on the back.
setup.caption: 3. Pick the riskiest and draw a plan to make it safer.

flow.do: Walk through the kitchen with your child and a grown-up. Point out five hazards, such as the gas stove, a sharp tool, a hot pan, a wet floor and a plug point. Write each on a card.
flow.say: Let us look for hazards in our kitchen. A hazard is anything that could cause harm. Can you find five? Do not touch them. Just point and name.
flow.kid: Walk through the kitchen. Name five hazards. Do not touch them.
flow.parent: Stay beside your child the whole time and keep them from touching anything on the list. The aim is to see, not to handle. Other good hazards are a glass jar on a high shelf, a steam cooker and a mat that slides.

flow.do: Take each card and ask: how likely is harm today, and how bad would it be? Write low, medium or high for the risk. Then say what would make the risk higher, and what would make it lower.
flow.say: A hazard is not the same as a risk. A risk is how likely the harm is, and how bad it would be. Is the risk of this one low, medium or high today? What would change that?
flow.kid: Rate each risk low, medium or high. Say what would change it.

ask.q: What would make the risk of this one higher today, and what would make it lower?
good: Higher with a hurry, a child nearby or a wet floor. Lower with a barrier, a grown-up present or the thing put away.

flow.parent: The same hazard can be low risk in one moment and high in another. A knife in a closed drawer is low risk. The same knife near the edge of the counter with a toddler about is higher. Let your child argue each rating. There may be more than one honest answer.

flow.do: Pick the card with the highest risk. Choose a plan for it. Decide which kind it is: remove, swap, separate or protect. Draw the plan on the back of the card. Say if there is a stronger kind of plan.
flow.say: Pick the riskiest one. Can you remove it, swap it, put a barrier or distance round it, or only protect yourself? Which of these is the strongest? Draw your plan.
flow.kid: Pick the riskiest card. Draw a plan. Say what kind it is.
flow.parent: The strongest kind of plan removes the hazard. Then comes a swap, then a barrier or distance, and last protection that you wear. A pan that must be hot cannot be removed, so you might keep a child away and have the grown-up cook. Let your child make the choice.
flow.think: Which of your plans changes the hazard, and which only changes the person?

projects.title: A week of drying forecasts: how well can you predict a wet cloth?
projects.context: In this project you time how long a wet cloth takes to dry and predict the next days' times. Then you predict for a new place, and you see how big the natural spread is from day to day.

schedule.what: List the risks. Wet, wring and hang the cloth. Check every hour until dry.
Predict from Day 1. Hang the cloth again in the same place and check every hour.
Predict from Days 1 and 2. Hang the cloth and check every hour.
Predict for a new place. Hang the cloth there and check every hour.
Find the spread of Days 1 to 3 and judge each prediction.
Draw the graph and write what you learned.

projects.record: Keep a table with the day, the place, your prediction, your reason and the time the cloth took to dry. Add the spread and the miss for each day. Draw a graph of predictions and results.
projects.safety: Hang the cloth at head height or lower. Do not climb or lean over a balcony rail to reach a line. Wipe up any water on the floor.

materials.item: two small cotton cloths of the same size
a bowl of water
a place to hang them at head height
a clock or phone
a kitchen scale (optional)
paper, a pen and graph paper

setup.art: A bowl of water with a cotton cloth in it and a hand wringing another cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Wet the cloth. Twist it ten times to wring it.

setup.art: A cloth hanging at head height from a low line, with a clock beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Hang it at head height. Write down the time.

setup.art: A hand touching a cloth to check if it is dry, with a notebook beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Check every hour until the cloth is dry.

setup.art: A graph with crosses for predictions and dots for results over six days.
setup.caption: 4. Draw your predictions and results on one graph.

flow.do: Choose one small cotton cloth, such as a handkerchief. Wet it in a bowl of water for one minute, then twist it ten times to wring it out. Hang it at head height in the spot you chose. Write the time. Check it every hour until it feels dry. Write down the time.
flow.say: How long will a wet cloth take to dry? Write a risk list first. Hang the cloth low, where nobody must climb or lean. Then guess the time, with a reason, and check every hour.
flow.kid: List the risks. Wet the cloth, wring it and hang it. Check every hour.
flow.parent: Risks to name: a wet floor under the line, climbing to reach a high line, and leaning over a balcony rail. Hang the cloth at head height or lower, with a cloth or tray underneath. A cloth is dry when it feels exactly like a dry cloth of the same kind, judged by the same person each day. With a kitchen scale you can weigh the cloth each hour, and it is dry when two weighings in a row match. In a very humid week the cloth may stay damp into the night. Then hang it in front of a fan, in the same place on every day, and write the time you checked. A chair back or a door handle also works for hanging.
flow.wait: Check once an hour until the cloth is dry

flow.do: Wet, wring and hang the cloth in the same spot in the same way. Before you hang it, write a prediction for the drying time using Day 1, with a reason. Check every hour. Write the time it dried.
flow.say: Yesterday the cloth took this long. How long do you think it will take today? Write your number and your reason in ink before you hang it.
flow.kid: Write a prediction. Hang the cloth. Check every hour.
flow.parent: Use the same cloth, the same twist and the same place. The weather may differ from day to day. That is what makes a spread.

flow.do: Repeat Day 2 exactly. Predict first, using Days 1 and 2. Then write the time it dried.
flow.say: Now you have two days of data. Can you predict better? Write the number and reason first.
flow.kid: Predict from two days. Hang the cloth. Check every hour.
flow.parent: Do not tell your child how good the prediction was until the cloth is dry.

flow.do: Choose a new place for the cloth, such as a shady corner or a window with sun. Predict the drying time there, with a reason from Days 1 to 3. Then wet, wring and hang the cloth in the new place, and check every hour.
flow.say: This place is new. What stays the same, and what changes? Write your number and your reason before you start.
flow.kid: Predict for the new place. Hang the cloth there. Check every hour.
flow.parent: A sunny place should be quicker and a shady one slower, but the size of the change is not obvious. This is a prediction about something unfamiliar, so a miss is expected and useful.

flow.do: Find the middle time and the spread of Days 1 to 3. Compare each of your predictions with the result, and say which were inside the spread. Then compare the new place's prediction with its result.
flow.say: The three days differ from each other. That wobble is the spread. Which of your predictions were inside it? What did the new place teach you?
flow.kid: Find the spread of Days 1 to 3. Judge each of your predictions.
flow.parent: If the days differ a lot, the weather probably changed. A forecast cannot be sharper than the natural spread of what it forecasts.

flow.do: Draw a graph with the days across and the drying time up. Mark each prediction with a cross and each result with a dot. Write what you learned about predicting, and what you would measure differently.
flow.say: Look at your crosses and your dots. Were they close? Did your predictions get better? What would help you predict better next time?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Write what you learned.
flow.parent: A good write-up says which of the three places, the doing, the tool or the reason, explained the biggest miss.
flow.think: Is a forecast of 'it will dry by evening' close enough, or do you need it to the minute? What decides?

challenges.title: A test station that survives a spill
challenges.context: A full cup of water will get knocked over sometime. You build a test station that keeps the spill from reaching the floor, a phone and your notebook.
challenges.problem: Build a test station where a knocked-over cup does not make the floor, the phone or the notebook wet. There is more than one good way.
constraints: Use only things from the home. No glass.
The test must still be possible to do at the station. You must be able to reach the cup.
Use only 100 millilitres of water in the tipping test.
Test your station at least twice.
general: Put the cup on a tray with a rim, and a towel under the tray.
Put the phone in a clear plastic bag and the notebook on the far side of the table.
Use a cup with a wide base that is harder to knock over.
creative: Work in a sink or a large bowl, so a spill goes straight to a drain.
Press a damp cloth round the base of the cup like a collar, so that spilled water is soaked up straight away.
Put the whole test inside a box lid lined with a bag, so the whole station is a tray.
challenges.your_turn: Build a station of your own from things at home. What did you change after the first tip that made the water do less harm? Do you think any station is ever spill-proof?

materials.item: a tray, a baking dish or a box lid
a plastic bag
a towel or old cloth
a small plastic cup with 100 millilitres of water
a phone and a notebook

setup.art: A tray with a rim holding a clear cup, with a phone in a plastic bag on a shelf above.
setup.caption: 1. Plan where the cup, the phone and the notebook will stand.

setup.art: A tray on a towel with a cup being tipped, and water pooling inside the rim of the tray.
setup.caption: 2. Tip a little water on purpose to copy a knock.

setup.art: A baking dish and a box lid lined with a plastic bag standing as two other designs.
setup.caption: 3. Try a second design and compare it.

flow.do: Read the problem and the rules. Draw a quick plan of your station. Say where the cup will stand, what will catch a spill, and where the phone and notebook will go.
flow.say: A cup of water will be knocked over one day. Where will the water go? Can you build a station so it does no harm? Draw your plan first.
flow.kid: Read the problem. Draw your plan. Say where the water will go.
flow.parent: Do not suggest a plan. Ask what the water would touch first and where it would run.

flow.do: Build your station from things in the house. Put in the cup, the phone in a plastic bag, the notebook and a cloth. Check that nothing is on the table edge.
flow.say: Build your station. Where will you put the phone and the notebook so they stay dry?
flow.kid: Build your station with things from home. Keep the phone dry.
flow.parent: Good ideas: a baking dish, a box lid lined with a plastic bag, a tray on a towel, or a dish rack in a sink. A cup that is not on the edge cuts the chance of a spill.

flow.do: Pour 100 millilitres of water into the cup, about half a small cup. Then tip the cup over its edge by hand, to copy a knock. Look at where the water went. Wipe up at once.
flow.say: Now we knock it over, on purpose, with a small amount of water. Where does the water go? Is anything wet that should be dry?
flow.kid: Tip a little water on purpose. Where did it go?
flow.parent: Use only 100 millilitres. Put a towel on the floor under the table first. Stay calm. A failure here is the useful part.

flow.do: Change one thing about your station so that the water does less harm. Tip a second time with 100 millilitres. Compare. Say which plan was the strongest kind: remove, swap, separate or protect.
flow.say: What did you change? Did it help? Which kind of plan is it?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Tip again. Did it help?
flow.parent: Another group may find a very different answer. Both can be good.
flow.think: Which of your changes removed a hazard, and which only caught a spill after it happened?

challenges.safety: Use only 100 millilitres of water, and put a towel on the floor first. Wipe up spills at once. Keep water away from plugs and sockets, and keep the phone in its bag.

challenges.title: Make your own measuring cup from a bottle
challenges.context: This is a design problem about measuring. You check your home-made cup against a real one and find where it is least exact.
challenges.problem: Turn a clear plastic bottle into a measuring cup with a mark every 25 millilitres up to 200. Your marks must agree with a real measuring cup to within 10 millilitres. There is more than one good way.
constraints: Use a plastic bottle and no glass.
Use only tape, a pen, water and a trusted measure to mark it.
Check at least three of your marks against a real measuring cup.
Write down the error of each mark.
general: Pour a trusted 25 millilitres in at a time and mark each line on tape.
Use a bottle with straight sides, so equal amounts make equal gaps.
Mark from the bottom up, and read at eye level each time.
creative: Ask a grown-up to cut the top off a wide bottle to make a cup with a handle, then mark the inside.
Use a narrow clear tube or a long bottle, so each millilitre is a larger gap and the cup is more exact.
Mark a bottle in tablespoons or katoris, for a cooking cup in the family's own units.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own measuring cup from things at home. How did you make your marks closer to a real cup? Do you think any home-made tool is ever as good as a bought one?

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle with straight sides, such as a one-litre water bottle
a medicine cup or a syringe without a needle, with marks in millilitres
masking tape and a waterproof pen
a kitchen measuring cup
a tray and a cloth

setup.art: A clear plastic bottle standing on a table with a strip of tape at a water line and a medicine cup beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Pour 25 millilitres, mark the line and write the amount.

setup.art: A child's eye level with the water line in the bottle.
setup.caption: 2. Read each mark with your eye level with the water.

setup.art: A bottle poured into a kitchen measuring cup to check one of the marks.
setup.caption: 3. Check your marks against a real measuring cup.

flow.do: Read the problem. Choose your master measure, which is a tool whose amount you trust, such as a medicine cup marked in millilitres. Decide how small your smallest mark will be.
flow.say: A measuring cup is only as good as its marks. What will be your trusted measure? How small will your smallest mark be? Why?
flow.kid: Choose your trusted measure. Decide your smallest mark.
flow.parent: A sealed bottle of water that is labelled 500 millilitres can serve as a master for a big mark. A medicine cup serves for small marks. Ask which marks must be the most careful.

flow.do: Stand the clear bottle on a flat table. Pour 25 millilitres from the master measure into it. Put a strip of tape at the water line, and write the amount with a pen. Add 25 millilitres again and mark again. Repeat up to 200 millilitres.
flow.say: Pour one measure, mark the line, pour again and mark again. Keep your eye level with the water at each mark. Why?
flow.kid: Pour 25 millilitres. Mark the line. Repeat to 200.
flow.parent: Read each mark at eye level with the bottle on a flat table, never held in the hand. If the bottle has a curved base, begin counting only above the curve and mark the first line from there.

flow.do: Pour 100 millilitres from a kitchen measuring cup into your bottle. Mark where your bottle says 100 and see how far it is from the water line. Do the same for 50 and 150.
flow.say: Does your bottle agree with the real cup? How far off is it? Is the error the same at the bottom and the top?
flow.kid: Test your marks with a real measuring cup. How far off are they?

ask.q: How close is your cup to a real one, and where is it the least accurate?
good: Answers vary. Usually the marks near the curved base are least accurate.

flow.parent: A difference of under half a mark is good. If a mark is off, fix it by moving the tape and testing again.

flow.do: Use your cup to measure 75 millilitres of water twice, and pour each into a real cup. Write how far each is from 75. Then say how you could make a finer cup.
flow.say: Measure 75 millilitres with your cup and check it on the real one. Which part of your cup would you improve first?
flow.kid: Measure 75 millilitres. Check it. Say how you would improve your cup.
flow.parent: A thinner bottle has marks that are further apart for the same volume, so a narrow bottle gives a finer cup.
flow.think: Why does a narrower bottle give a more exact cup? What would a tool maker do to make a cup with marks every 1 millilitre?

challenges.safety: Only a grown-up cuts a bottle, and the cut edge is covered with tape, because cut plastic can be sharp. Use no glass. Wipe up water as you go.

worksheets.title: Tools, risks and predictions (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can choose and use tools, tell a hazard from a risk, and judge how close a prediction was.

items.p: Which tool answers 'How much water is in this tumbler?'
opts: A measuring cup
A ruler
A stopwatch
items.why: Water in a tumbler is a volume, and a measuring cup measures volume. A ruler measures length and a stopwatch measures time.

items.p: A thermometer measures ____.
items.why: Each tool measures one kind of quantity. A thermometer is built for temperature.

items.p: You press the zero button on a kitchen scale after putting the empty bowl on. Why?
opts: So the bowl weighs nothing in real life
To switch the scale on
So it shows only what you add
items.why: The bowl has a mass of its own. Setting zero with the bowl on lets the scale show the food alone.

items.p: A thermometer shows the true number the moment it touches the water.
items.why: False. A thermometer needs about a minute for its number to stop changing. Read it after it settles.

items.p: Match each job to the tool that fits it.
pairs: How long a toy car rolls
How much milk fits in a glass
items.why: Each job asks about one quantity: time, length, volume or temperature. Each tool is made to measure one of them.

items.p: Sort each one into hazard or plan to cut a risk.
items: a plastic cup in place of glass
items.why: A hazard is a thing that could cause harm. A plan changes the set-up, so that harm is less likely or smaller.

items.p: A spill on the floor is a hazard. Which makes the risk of a slip smaller?
opts: Leaving it until the test ends
Wiping it up at once
Walking round it faster
items.why: Wiping removes the hazard from where people walk. Leaving it or hurrying past keeps the chance of a slip high.

items.p: Put these steps of a safe test in order.
a: Set up the tray and tools
items.why: Risks come first, so the set-up can include their plans. Then you work. Tidying and washing close the test.

items.p: If something unexpected happens in a test, keep going and fix it afterwards.
items.why: False. A plan cannot cover everything. Stop, step back, tell someone and think before you carry on.

items.p: A prediction says what you expect, and it also gives a ____.
items.why: The reason lets others check your thinking. If the result differs, it shows what to look at again.

items.p: You predicted 30 seconds. The result was 36 seconds. What is the difference?
opts: 66 seconds
30 seconds
6 seconds
items.why: Subtract the smaller from the larger. 36 minus 30 is 6. Adding the two numbers is a common slip.

items.p: Two predictions missed by 12 seconds. One result was 30 seconds, the other 10 minutes. Which miss matters more?
opts: The 10-minute one
The 30-second one
They matter the same
items.why: 12 seconds is a large share of 30 seconds and a tiny share of 10 minutes. Compare a miss with the size of the result.

items.p: The big ice cube was predicted to melt first, but the small one did. Name two places to look for the cause.
items.a: A good answer names two places. The doing: were the cubes in the same water and place? The tool: was the same clock used? The reason: is the idea that bigger means first wrong?
items.why: A miss can come from how the test was done, from the equipment, or from the idea behind the prediction. Check the first two before blaming the idea.

items.p: Draw a tray, three cups and a spill cloth. Mark where a baby or pet should not be.
items.a: A tray in the middle of a table with three cups on it. A cloth beside it. A cross where a small child or pet could reach.
items.why: A tray and a clear space are barriers. They keep a spill and small hands away from each other.

items.p: Predict how long a wet sock takes to dry on a line, and give a reason from something you have seen.
items.a: A time such as 'about 3 hours'. A reason from something seen, such as 'a wet shirt took that long yesterday'.
items.why: A prediction without a reason is only a guess. Reasons come from patterns you have watched before.

items.p: Two ways to plan a test that needs warm water.

views.who: A parent who wants no warm water at all (an imagined view)
views.says: Use cold water only. The hazard is gone, and cold water still shows how fast sugar dissolves.

views.who: A teacher who allows warm tap water with a grown-up pouring (an imagined view)
views.says: Use warm tap water. The difference between cold and warm is bigger and easier to see, and the risk is small if a grown-up pours.

items.ask: Which would you choose for your home, and what would you lose with the other one?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says removing the hazard is the strongest plan. It also says the warm test teaches more but needs a grown-up and a tray, so it is a trade-off.
items.why: Both views are sensible. The first is the stronger kind of plan. The second accepts a small risk for a clearer result, and that is a choice people make differently.

worksheets.title: Plans, spread and misses (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to use a hundred grains, a thermometer and the spread to judge predictions and plans in new situations.

items.p: You want the mass of one grain of rice on a scale that shows whole grams. What works?
opts: Weigh one grain and round up
Weigh a hundred grains, then divide
Use a bigger scale
items.why: One grain is far below the scale's smallest mark. A hundred grains give a reading you can see, and dividing by a hundred gives one grain.

items.p: 100 grains of rice weigh 2 grams. What is the mass of one grain, in grams?
items.why: 2 divided by a hundred is 0.02 grams. This is how a tool that is too coarse for one grain can still tell you about it.

items.p: Holding a thermometer by its tip gives the most exact reading.
items.why: False. The tip then feels your fingers and not the water. Hold the thermometer by its top end.

items.p: A thermometer reads 44, then 42, then settles at 41 after a minute. Which do you write down?
items.why: The reading changes until the thermometer has taken on the water's temperature. The settled number is the real reading.

items.p: A glass jar can break. In which set-up is the risk highest?
opts: Standing on a mat on a table
Carried quickly across a tiled floor
Inside a closed cupboard
items.why: The hazard is the same in all three. The risk rises with speed, a hard floor and a chance of dropping it.

items.p: Match each plan to its kind.
pairs: Use cold water because the test works without warmth
Use warm tap water in place of boiling water
Keep a baby in another room
items.why: Remove takes the hazard away. Swap makes it safer. Separate keeps people away from it. Protect only guards your body.

items.p: Sort each plan by when it happens.
items: step back and tell someone about a surprise
items.why: A plan on paper protects nobody unless the hands follow it. Some steps are done in advance, and some are habits for the moment.

items.p: You have timed ice cubes melting. Which prediction for crushed ice of the same mass has the best reason?
opts: Faster, because more ice touches the water
The same, because ice is ice
Nobody can say before trying it
items.why: Step from the known case. Crushed ice has the same ice but much more surface touching the water, so it should melt sooner.

items.p: Runs of 20, 24 and 22 seconds. You predicted 21. Was the prediction accurate?
opts: No, none of the runs was 21
No, it was lower than the middle run
Yes, it lies inside the spread
items.why: The three runs spread over 4 seconds. A prediction inside that spread is as close as the test can judge.

items.p: You predicted 50 seconds and the result was 40 seconds. The prediction was too ____.
items.why: Saying which way you missed helps: 50 was longer than 40, so you expected the sugar to be slower than it was.

items.p: You predicted 40 seconds and the result was 50. The miss is what fraction of the result?
items.why: The difference is 10. 10 out of 50 is 1/5, which is 20 in every 100.

items.p: Put these in order for judging a prediction.
a: Find the spread of the runs
Compare the miss with the spread
items.why: The prediction must come first, or hindsight changes it. Repeated runs give the spread, and only then can a miss be judged.

items.p: Your sugar took twice as long as predicted. List your three checks in order, with one thing to look for in each.
items.a: The doing: were all the cups stirred the same? The tool: was the spoon level each time? The reason: is something other than warmth, such as crystal size, also at work?
items.why: Check the doing and the tool first, since they are easier to fix. Then question the idea behind the prediction.

items.p: If a result matches your prediction, your reason is proved right.
items.why: False. A different reason could give the same number. A match means the reason passed one test, and the next test can still go against it.

items.p: A farmer and an engineer both use a forecast. Each must decide how close is close enough.

views.who: A farmer planning when to sow (an imagined view)
views.says: A forecast that may be off by about 5 in every 100 is close enough. I can plan around that.

views.who: An engineer cutting a part for a machine (an imagined view)
views.says: A miss of 5 in every 100 would ruin the part. I need a far smaller miss.

items.ask: Is either of them wrong? What decides how close is close enough?
items.a: Neither is wrong. A strong answer says the purpose decides, because a sowing plan can absorb a miss that a machine part cannot.
items.why: How close is close enough depends on the natural spread of the results and on what the answer is for.

items.p: Draw a risk list with three columns for a test with a steel bowl of warm water. Fill one row.
items.a: Three columns headed What could hurt, Who could be hurt, and My plan. One row such as: a spill makes the floor slippery, anyone walking by, a tray and a cloth.
items.why: A risk assessment asks what could hurt, who, and what to do. Writing it down makes each answer clear.

items.p: To test which food ants like, name one risk to the ants and one plan to reduce it.
items.a: A risk such as crushing, trapping or flooding the ants. A plan such as watching them where they already walk, putting a tiny grain of food near their path, and not shutting them in a jar.
items.why: The risk assessment counts every living being the test touches, not only people. Ants feel and decide too, so they are on the list.

worksheets.title: Faulty checks and open questions (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet tests faulty reasoning about predictions and risks, and asks questions that have no single answer.

items.p: Both predicted 30 seconds. Child A got 29, 31 and 30. Child B got 18, 42 and 30. Who is better supported?
opts: Child A, whose runs cluster tightly
Child B, because 30 was one of the runs
Both the same, since the middle is 30
items.why: A tight spread lets the prediction be judged sharply. A wide spread means the test itself cannot tell 30 from many other numbers.

items.p: A prediction that comes true proves that its reason is right.
items.why: False. Another reason could give the same number. A true prediction is one test passed, not a proof.

items.p: Warm water took longer than cold. The warm cup was stirred gently and the cold one hard. What is at fault?
opts: The reason, because warm water is slower
The doing, because stirring differed
The thermometer
items.why: Only the warmth should change. Different stirring is another change, so the test cannot say what caused the result.

items.p: A forecast says 80 centimetres of rain, plus or minus 5 per cent. 77 fall. Is that within the stated error?
opts: No, it was not exactly 80
No, because 77 is lower
Yes, 77 lies between 76 and 84
items.why: A forecast with a stated error is judged against that error. The range is 76 to 84, and 77 sits inside it.

items.p: Why does it matter to write a prediction in ink before the test?
items.a: A good answer says that after seeing a result, people remember expecting it, which is hindsight. A number in ink cannot change, so the miss can be judged honestly.
items.why: Hindsight makes a result feel more expected than it was. A written prediction beats memory.

items.p: A risk list names a scald, a slip and a broken cup. The test uses an untested powder. What is missing?
opts: Nothing, because three risks are enough
Treating the powder as hazardous until tested
Nothing, because powders are always safe
items.why: A list covers only the hazards known at the time. A new material is treated as hazardous until tests show it is not, and that is why we never taste in a test.

items.p: Sort each test by whether it is worth its risk.
items: a grown-up cutting an apple to watch it turn brown
using water at full boil when warm tap water works just as well
growing seeds on a window sill
tasting an unknown powder to see what it is
items.why: The question is never only 'is it safe'. It is how big the risk is, what the test gives, and whether a safer way does the same job.

items.p: Match each job to how big a miss it can accept.
pairs: A recipe that says 'about a cup'
Taking an umbrella for tomorrow's rain
Cutting a part for a rocket engine
items.why: What counts as close enough depends on what the answer is used for, and on how bad a wrong answer would be.

items.p: Two weather computers start from nearly the same numbers. Ten days on, their forecasts differ greatly. Why?
opts: Tiny differences at the start grow in weather
One computer must be broken
Weather has no rules at all
items.why: Weather follows fixed laws, but small differences in the start grow into large ones. So the forecast gets worse with each day ahead.

items.p: Give a reason to predict the Sun will rise tomorrow without saying 'it always has'.
items.a: Answers vary. A good one says the Earth spins and keeps spinning unless something stops it, and we understand why the Sun seems to rise. The prediction comes from a cause, not only from the past.
items.why: A reason made only of past days could not tell a lucky run from a rule. A cause we understand gives a stronger prediction.

items.p: A prediction missed. Two scientists look at it differently.

views.who: A scientist who keeps the rule and looks for a hidden cause (an imagined view)
views.says: The rule has worked everywhere else. Something unseen must be pulling the result off, and I will search for it.

views.who: A scientist who doubts the rule itself (an imagined view)
views.says: A rule that keeps missing in the same way may be wrong or incomplete. I will test changing the rule.

items.ask: How could more tests tell these two apart?
items.a: Answers vary. A good one says that finding the hidden cause would settle the first view, and that a new rule predicting better would settle the second. Until then both can be reasonable.
items.why: History holds both: sometimes the hidden cause was found, and sometimes the rule needed changing. A miss alone cannot say which.

items.p: Draw one bowl of warm water twice, with a high-risk and a low-risk set-up. Label three differences.
items.a: High risk: a bowl at the table edge, no tray, a toddler close by. Low risk: a bowl on a tray in the middle of a cleared table, a cloth ready, a grown-up near and the toddler in another room.
items.why: The hazard is the same in both drawings. The risk changes with where the bowl is, what is under it and who is near.

items.p: A thermometer reads 44, then 41 after a minute, then stays at 41. Record ____ degrees.
items.why: The thermometer needs about a minute to settle. The number that stops changing is the water's temperature.

items.p: Checklists are only for beginners, because experts do not forget steps.
items.why: False. Experts forget simple steps too, most of all when the work is familiar. Checklists catch the slips that skill does not.

items.p: Think of a guess of yours that missed. Which place explains it best: the doing, the tool or the reason?
items.a: Answers vary. A good answer names a real moment, picks one of the three places, and gives a reason for the choice.
items.why: Asking where a miss came from turns a surprise into something to learn.

items.p: You must time a snap that lasts 0.3 seconds. Why is timing it by hand a poor choice?
opts: A 0.2 second reaction is most of 0.3
Phones cannot show tenths of a second
Such short times do not exist
items.why: A person needs about a fifth of a second to react. For a very short event, that delay is a large share of the whole time.

quiz.p: You must find how much water fits in a bottle cap. Which tool fits best?
opts: A one-litre jug marked every 100 millilitres
A school ruler
A medicine cup marked every 1 millilitre
quiz.why: A tool's smallest mark must be much smaller than your amount. The jug's smallest mark is far bigger than a cap of water, and a ruler measures length, not volume.

quiz.p: A 15 centimetre ruler is used to measure a 6 metre room. What is the main problem?
opts: Laying it down 40 times adds 40 small mistakes
Its marks are too big
A ruler cannot measure length
quiz.why: A tool that is too fine for the job adds many small mistakes. A tape would fit the job. The ruler's marks are tiny, and it does measure length, but only well over short distances.

quiz.p: Water in a measuring cup looks higher from above than from the side. Which reading is right?
opts: The one from above
The one with your eye level
The average of the two
quiz.why: Looking from above makes the water seem to stand at a different mark. Eye level is the one position that gives the true mark.

quiz.p: A ruler's zero is 2 millimetres in from its end. You start measuring a pencil at the end, not at zero. The reading is...
opts: 2 millimetres too big
2 millimetres too small
exactly right
quiz.why: The scale starts counting 2 millimetres in from the end. So the first 2 millimetres of the pencil lie before the zero mark and are never counted. The reading is 2 millimetres less than the true length. Always line up the zero mark and not the edge.

quiz.p: Which sentence about a knife is true?
opts: A hazard only in someone's hand
A hazard in a drawer, with a low risk
A risk in a drawer only
quiz.why: A hazard is what could cause harm, so the knife is one everywhere. The risk is the chance and size of the harm, and that changes with how and where it is used.

quiz.p: Why list the risks of a test before starting it?
opts: It proves the test is perfectly safe
It makes the test finish sooner
A named risk is easier to plan for
quiz.why: Naming a risk lets you plan a way to make it smaller. No test has zero risk, so a list can never prove perfect safety.

quiz.p: Put these ways to cut a risk in order, from strongest to weakest.
a: Swap it for a safer one
Put a barrier or distance between
quiz.why: Removing the hazard leaves nothing to go wrong. Swapping lowers it. A barrier keeps it away from people. Protection is weakest because the hazard is still there and the protection can slip.

quiz.p: A test works with cold water or with boiling water. Which plan cuts the risk most?
opts: Use cold water
Boiling water, poured slowly
Boiling water, with oven gloves
quiz.why: Cold water removes the scald hazard, and nothing is lost. Pouring slowly and gloves only make a hazard that is still there a little less likely to hurt.

quiz.p: Halfway through a test, a cup cracks. What do you do?
opts: Pick up the pieces quickly
Finish the run, then clear up
Stop, step back and fetch a grown-up
quiz.why: A plan cannot cover everything. When something unexpected happens, the safe habit is to stop and think before the hands carry on.

quiz.p: Which of these is a prediction and not only a guess?
opts: Warm water will be quicker
Quicker, because cold took longer than room-warm
It will take about 30 seconds
quiz.why: A prediction carries a reason taken from what you know. The reason lets others check your thinking and tells you what to rethink if the result differs.

quiz.p: You have timed sugar but never rock salt. What is the best first step to predict for rock salt?
opts: Compare what rock salt shares with sugar
Say nobody can predict a new thing
Pick any number, because it is new
quiz.why: Predicting the new works by stepping from a familiar case. Both dissolve, so warm should help, and rock salt crystals are bigger, so it may be slower.

quiz.p: You predict 25 seconds. Three runs give 31, 34 and 37 seconds. Judged by the spread, was the prediction accurate?
opts: No, 25 is outside the runs' spread
Yes, because 25 is near 31
Yes, any number under 40 is fine
quiz.why: The runs differ by 6 seconds without anything being wrong. A prediction outside that spread is a real miss, and 25 is 6 seconds below the lowest run. A number is not fine only because it is small.

quiz.p: Writing your prediction after you see the result is as good as writing it before.
quiz.why: False. After people see a result, they honestly remember having expected it. A number written before the test cannot change.

quiz.p: A prediction missed by a lot. Which check comes first?
opts: Whether each run was done the same way
Whether the idea behind it is wrong
Whether the thermometer is lying
quiz.why: Look at the doing first, then the tool, then the reason. The first two are easier to fix, and each is a likelier cause than a wrong idea.

quiz.p: Two planets strayed from the sums. For one, an unseen planet was found. For the other, none ever was. What does that show?
opts: A miss always means a hidden object
A prediction that missed is useless
A miss alone cannot say what is wrong
quiz.why: In one case the cause was hidden outside the idea. In the other the idea itself needed changing. A miss is a clue. Further tests are needed to tell which.

applications: On the news in June, listen for the monsoon forecast from the India Meteorological Department. It comes as a percentage of the long-term average, and it may be off by about 5 per cent. Farmers plan sowing around it.

Cyclone warnings on the Odisha and Tamil Nadu coasts rely on predicting where a cyclone will land. In 2013 a good forecast helped about a million people move inland before Cyclone Phailin. Look at a cyclone warning on your phone and notice the 'cone' that shows how wide the forecast spread is.
A cough syrup comes with a small measuring cup because a kitchen spoon varies in size. Read the dose on a bottle and see which mark the cup shows. A miss here matters much more than in a recipe.
Surgeons in many hospitals read a short checklist aloud before an operation. Ask a parent if they have seen a checklist at a hospital or in a clinic, and what it asked.
Rocket launches everywhere use a long checklist during the countdown, because one forgotten step can end the mission. Watch a launch video and listen for the calls and replies.
A tailor measures twice before cutting cloth, with a tape that fits the job. Watch a tailor and notice what the tape measures and what a mistake would cost.
A weighing scale at a shop shows grams, and a grocer weighs 100 grams of a spice by sight first, then checks. Notice how close the first guess is each time.

spotted.text: When a parent tests whether the dosa pan is hot by sprinkling a few drops of water, watch what the drops do. They sizzle and dance when the pan is ready. That is a quick test with a prediction inside it.
spotted.art: A hand sprinkling water drops onto a dosa pan, with the drops dancing.

spotted.text: Look at the marks on a milk pouch, a medicine bottle cap and a one-litre jug. Find the smallest mark on each and say which could measure 5 millilitres.
spotted.art: A medicine cup, a jug and a milk pouch side by side with their marks circled.
