spotted.text: On the way to school, look for something that keeps people away from a hazard. It might be a railing at a drain, a fence round a pond, a speed bump or a zebra crossing. Say whether it removes, swaps, separates or protects.
spotted.art: A street with a railing at a drain and a zebra crossing, with arrows pointing to each.

spotted.text: Watch a cook check sugar syrup between two fingers, or a potter check a pot's dryness by touch. Each one has a test and a prediction learned from hands that have done it many times.
spotted.art: A cook holding a drop of syrup between a finger and thumb.

spotted.text: Look at a packing list on a fridge or a school timetable stuck on a wall. Each is a kind of checklist. Notice what it saves you from forgetting.
spotted.art: A school bag beside a timetable with ticks next to some lines.

spotted.text: When the evening news gives tomorrow's forecast, write down what it says. Tomorrow, check the weather and say whether the forecast was close enough for what you needed to do.
spotted.art: A television showing a weather map, with a notebook beside it.

spotted.text: Watch how a grown-up checks the gas knob before leaving the kitchen. This one-line checklist guards against a hazard that skill alone can forget.

ask_kids: What is the hazard in your kitchen that worries you most, and what is the risk of it today? How would you make it smaller?
You may take only one tool to a test: a stopwatch, a ruler or a thermometer. Which would you choose? What could it never tell you?
Your two hands disagreed about the same water. Which other things in your day depend on what you have just felt before?
When you guess the weather for tomorrow, what do you use for your reason? How close are you usually?
If a prediction of yours missed, how could you find out whether the doing, the tool or the idea was at fault?
How could you make a test safer for the ants or plants taking part?
Think of a small risk you took, such as climbing a tree. What did you gain? Who else could have been hurt?
Is there something you can predict very well, and something you cannot? What makes the difference?

maths.problem: Three timed runs of the sugar test give 48, 52 and 56 seconds. Find the mean by adding and dividing by 3, and the spread, which is the biggest minus the smallest. Is a prediction of 50 inside the spread?
maths.answer: Mean 52 seconds. Spread 8 seconds. Yes, 50 lies between 48 and 56.
maths.explain: 48 + 52 + 56 = 156. 156 ÷ 3 = 52. The biggest is 56 and the smallest is 48, and 56 − 48 = 8. A prediction between 48 and 56 is inside the spread, so the test cannot tell it from the truth.
maths.context: This problem uses the numbers of a dissolving test to find the average and the spread, and to judge a prediction.
maths.why_maths: A mean and a spread are the two numbers a scientist needs to say how close a prediction was. One run alone cannot give either.

maths.problem: One test predicted 40 seconds and got 52. Another predicted 9 minutes and got 10 minutes. Which miss is bigger in seconds, and which is bigger as a share of its result?
maths.answer: The 9-minute test misses by more seconds (60 against 12). The 40-second test misses by the bigger share, about 23 per cent against 10 per cent.
maths.explain: First test: 52 − 40 = 12 seconds. 12 ÷ 52 is about 0.23, which is 23 per cent. Second test: 10 minutes is 600 seconds and 9 minutes is 540, so the miss is 60 seconds. 60 ÷ 600 = 0.1, which is 10 per cent.
maths.context: This problem compares two misses by their size in seconds and by their share of the result.
maths.why_maths: A miss only means something when it is compared with the size of the result. This is how a forecast is judged.

maths.problem: A jug is marked every 100 millilitres, so a reading may be off by up to 50 millilitres. A medicine cup is marked every 5 millilitres, so a reading may be off by up to 2.5. How many times smaller is the cup's possible error?
maths.explain: The error can be up to half of the smallest mark. 50 ÷ 2.5 = 20. For a 10 millilitre amount, an error of 50 is five times the amount itself, so the jug is useless for it.
maths.context: This problem turns the idea of the smallest mark into a number.
maths.why_maths: A tool can be wrong by about half of its smallest mark. Comparing marks is how you choose a tool that fits the job.

maths.problem: A kitchen scale shows whole grams. 1,000 grains of rice show 21 grams. What is the mass of one grain? Why is weighing 1,000 grains better than weighing 100 grains that show 2 grams?
maths.answer: 0.021 grams. The scale's rounding of up to 0.5 gram is about 2 per cent of 21 grams, but about 25 per cent of 2 grams.
maths.explain: 21 ÷ 1,000 = 0.021. A reading of 2 grams may truly be anything from 1.5 to 2.5, a swing of 0.5 out of 2, which is 25 per cent. A reading of 21 swings 0.5 out of 21, about 2 per cent.
maths.context: This problem uses a coarse scale to find the mass of one grain, by weighing many together.
maths.why_maths: Weighing many and dividing shrinks the share of the rounding error. Scientists use the same trick whenever a tool is too coarse for one small thing.

maths.problem: A test has a one-in-a-hundred chance of a small spill and a one-in-ten-thousand chance of a cut. If 200 families do it, how many spills and cuts do you expect?
maths.answer: About 2 spills and 0.02 cuts. A cut is unlikely: about one chance in 50 that anyone is cut at all.
maths.explain: 200 × 1/100 = 2 spills. 200 × 1/10,000 = 0.02, which is about one chance in 50. A risk joins how likely a harm is with how bad it would be. Spills are likely and mild. A cut is unlikely and worse.
maths.context: This problem puts numbers on how likely each harm is and compares two risks.
maths.why_maths: A risk is a chance times a size. Counting how many times something is expected to happen across many tries is how safety workers compare risks.

maths.problem: A hand-timed run has a finger error of 0.2 seconds at the stop only. How big is that error as a share of a 5-second event, and of a 0.5-second event?
maths.answer: 4 per cent of 5 seconds, and 40 per cent of 0.5 seconds.
maths.explain: 0.2 ÷ 5 = 0.04, which is 4 per cent. 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = 0.4, which is 40 per cent. The same error is small for a long event and huge for a short one.
maths.context: This problem uses the delay found with the falling ruler to judge hand timing for long and short events.
maths.why_maths: An error only matters compared with the size of the thing being timed. This is why very short events are timed by cameras.

warmup.q: Which tool tells you how hot water is?
Where should your eye be when you read a measuring cup?
warmup.a: Level with the water, looking straight across.

warmup.q: What is the difference between a hazard and a risk?
warmup.a: A hazard is anything that could cause harm. A risk is how likely the harm is, and how bad.

warmup.q: A prediction has two parts. What are they?
warmup.a: What you expect to happen, and a reason.

warmup.q: You predict 30 seconds and the result is 36. What is the difference?
Name the strongest way to cut a risk.
Why do we run a test three times?
warmup.a: One run can be a fluke, and the spread of three runs shows how much results wobble.

warmup.q: Why write your prediction before the test and not after?
warmup.a: After a result is known, people remember expecting it. A written number cannot change.

quiz: Every measuring tool is built to measure one kind of quantity.
A ruler measures length, a cup measures volume and a thermometer measures temperature.
You should read a measuring cup by looking down from above.
Looking down from above shifts where the water line seems to be. Bend down to eye level.
A hazard is the same as a risk.
A hazard is what could cause harm. A risk is how likely the harm is, and how bad.
Wearing protection is the strongest way to cut a risk.
It is the weakest. The hazard is still there, and protection can slip.
Removing a hazard is stronger than swapping it for a safer one.
If the hazard is gone, nothing can go wrong. A swap leaves a smaller hazard.
A prediction needs a reason as well as a guess.
The reason lets others check your thinking and shows what to rethink if the result differs.
No test can ever have zero risk.
Even cold water on a floor can be slipped on. People choose how much risk is fine.
If a result is not what you predicted, the idea must be wrong.
The doing or the tool may be at fault. Check those two first.
A thermometer shows its true number at the very instant you put it in.
It takes about a minute to settle, so read it then.
A repeated test gives exactly the same number every time.
Results wobble, and the size of the wobble is the spread.
odd: The others measure length. A thermometer measures temperature.
Cold water in place of warm
The others make a risk smaller. A spill is the hazard.
Time, volume and mass are quantities with units. Risk is a chance joined to a size.
The others are ways to cut a risk. A guess is the start of a prediction.
The others are what a good prediction does. Changing it after hides the miss.
